Budynek ceglany datowany na połowę XIV wieku, silnie przebudowany w XVI (przebudowa wzmiankowana w 1526 roku, a następnie w latach 1558–1561), XIX wieku (m.in. 1850, 1861–1862, 1865, 1879, 1889–1892) i w latach 1925–1929 (rekonstrukcja niektórych elementów detalu architektonicznego), w 1947 roku i w latach 1964–1968. W trakcie tych ostatnich działań przeprowadzono generalny remont „pod kątem przywrócenia stanu z XVI wieku” na cele ekspozycji muzealnej (rekompozycja elewacji frontowej, zmiana ułożenia otworów okiennych, przeniesienie portalu głównego, wymiana sterczyn, strop gęstożebrowy nad Salą Pospólstwa). Ratusz zyskał manierystyczną szatę stylową w latach 1558–1561. W piwnicach ratusza była m.in. zbrojownia, na parterze występowały sklepione pomieszczenia (wietnica, mieszkania instygatora miejskiego i wietnika itp.), na piętrze m.in. Sala Pospólstwa (zmieniona w 1793 roku w mniejsze pomieszczenia) i Sala Rady. Budynek uległ dotkliwym pożarom m.in. w 1663 i 1792 roku. Po tej drugiej pożodze został odbudowany, jednak wewnątrz obniżono sufity i zmieniono organizację pomieszczeń. W latach 1861–1862 odkopano piwnice ratuszowe (nieużywane od XVIII wieku), wyburzono zachodni narożnik wagi miejskiej (rozebrana całkowicie w latach kolejnego remontu), a cały budynek poddano doraźnemu remontowi. Gruntownym remontem i zmianą dekoracji na neorenesansową w latach 1889–1892 kierował Szczęsny Zaremba. Obecna zabudowa wokół Rynku Głównego jest znacznie uboższa niż przed pożarem miasta w 1663 roku, jednak wiele stojących dzisiaj kamienic rynkowych posiada XIV-, XVi XVI-wieczne piwnice, np. w kamienicy Ratajewiczowskiej są datowane na XIV wiek. Powolna odbudowa miasta pozostającego w kryzysie, łączenie działek i kolejne pożary sprawiły, że budynki zmieniały swój wygląd. Okazałe renesansowe kamienice z podcieniami zastąpiły skromne kamienice czynszowe, a pozostałe po pożogach i odbudowach podcienia z czasem całkowicie usunięto lub przebudowano – odtworzono w trakcie prac restauratorsko-konserwatorskich w XX wieku podcienia w kamienicy Rosowskich, Sakowiczowskiej, Rynek 14 oraz między kamienicami Rynek 19–21. Pod koniec XVIII i w pierwszych dekadach XIX wieku po pożarach w wielu kamienicach dobudowano drugie piętro. Wówczas też zyskały nową szatę stylową, jak np. kamienica Nikielsonowska, którą zamieniono w szerokofrontową kamienicę z dekoracją klasycystyczną. Na przełomie XIX i XX wieku nastąpiły kolejne przebudowy kamienic, spośród których wiele zyskało historyzujące elewacje. Obiekt wznoszony od XIV wieku w miejscu poprzedniego jako jednonawowa świątynia parafialna z zamkniętym prostokątnie prezbiterium, powiększana po 1400 roku o (prawdopodobnie) wieżę, dwie kaplice (zakrystyjną i św. Krzyża). Na początku XV wieku dobudowano kaplicę św. Anny i piętrową kaplicę gotycką (przebudowana, nakryta kopułą i ozdobiona

dekoracją barokową w 1712 roku), a w 1415 roku kaplicę Rozesłania Apostołów. Kolejne rozbudowy trwały w latach 1485– 1514 z fundacji Jana Amora Tarnowskiego, kiedy to pojawiły się późnogotyckie portale i inne kamienne elementy wystroju architektonicznego, sklepienia (m.in. sieciowe w nawie z XVI wieku, uzupełniane w 1890 roku), a także nowa kaplica – Matki Boskiej Szkaplerznej (z ok. 1514 roku, ze sklepieniem krzyżowo-żebrowym) oraz skarbiec nad zakrystią. Kolegiata padała ofiarą pożarów m.in. w 1617, 1663 oraz 1735 roku, jednak ofiarność możnych i mieszczan umożliwiały naprawy i remonty zniszczonych części. W latach 1810–1816 i 1827–1832 świątynia została przekształcona z jednonawowej z kaplicami w trójnawową z arkadami między nawami, wydłużono prezbiterium i wybudowano neogotycką kaplicę św. Benedykta. W latach pięćdziesiątych XIX wieku zakupiono nowe ołtarze, wyłożono posadzkę i wystawiono zakrystię zw. kanonicką. Z inicjatywy biskupa Ignacego Łobosa w latach 1889–1897 architekt Julian Zachariewicz przygotował plan purystycznej restauracji katedry. Wtedy dobudowano m.in. ostatnie przęsło prezbiterium z wielobocznym zamknięciem, dwie północne kruchty oraz zwieńczenie wieży. Wówczas też nałożono neogotycką szatę stylową w duchu purystycznym. Obiekt wielokrotnie odnawiano, m.in. w latach 1926–1927, 1957–1960 (konserwacja nagrobków, wymiana oświetlenia i posadzki, wyeksponowanie okien gotyckich w prezbiterium, fresków wokół pomników Ostrogskich oraz polichromii gotycko-renesansowej w kaplicy Matki Boskiej Szkaplerznej), 1960–1962 (odnowienie polichromii i posadzki), 1983 (konserwacja i zabezpieczenie polichromii), 2005–2007 (wymiana dachu). Wytyczony już przy lokacji miasta w 1330 roku plac stanowi po chwilę obecną przestrzeń, w której dominantą jest katedra. Do najważniejszych zabudowań placu (poza bazyliką katedralną) należy m.in. scholasteria, akademiola, dom Mikołajowski, Kanonia I i Kanonia II, pałacyk kanonicki, a pomiędzy tymi obiektami nie brakuje zabudowań z XIX i XX wieku. Dom Mikołajowski stanowił własność m.in. Koruszowskich oraz Barbary i Jana Mikołajowskich herbu Gryf. Ci ostatni w 1524 roku dokonali jego znacznej przebudowy w duchu późnogotyckim. Po fundacji tzw. akademioli przez Wojciecha Kaszewicza w 1753 roku dom stał się mieszkaniem profesorów kolonii akademickiej, a po założeniu w 1792 roku w miejscu akademioli gimnazjum budynek został rezydencją prefekta gimnazjalnego. Przez kolejne dekady dom Mikołajowski pełnił funkcje szkolne i tymczasowo siedzibę ośrodka zdrowia, a po remoncie z lat 1946–1952 zamieniono go w przestrzeń wystawienniczą Muzeum Diecezjalnego. Sąsiadujący z nim Dom Mansjonarzy ma formę, którą nadano mu w XVIII wieku. Był poddawany pracom budowlano-adaptacyjnym (m.in. na potrzeby muzealne w latach sześćdziesiątych–dziewięćdziesiątych XX wieku), które obejmowały chociażby wykonanie klatki schodowej, wymianę stolarki okiennej i drzwiowej oraz dostosowanie konstrukcji stropu do potrzeb wystawienniczych. Murowany pałacyk kanonicki wzniósł jako piętrowy budynek przy murach obronnych ks. Mikołaj Zamoyski, a następnie gruntownie przebudował prepozyt Stanisław Świejkowski. Po rozbiorze

Rzeczypospolitej znajdowała się w nim siedziba władz cyrkularnych. W ostatnich dwóch dekadach XVIII wieku dobudowano do niego dwa skrzydła boczne i zorganizowano w jednym ze skrzydeł wozownię. W XIX wieku poddany gruntownemu remontowi, w trakcie którego elewacjom zewnętrznym nadano neorenesansowe formy. Kościół filialny pw. NMP Wniebowziętej „na Burku” (ob. sanktuarium MB Szkaplerznej) Obecna świątynia została wzniesiona na przedmieściach ok. 1458 roku, w miejscu poprzedniej. Konsekrowana w 1462 roku. Jednonawowa z węższym i zamkniętym trójbocznie prezbiterium z przylegającą doń od północy zakrystią z przedsionkiem. Od zachodu wieża. Kościół uległ znacznym zniszczeniom w trakcie pożaru na początku XVII wieku, odbudowano spalone partie przed 1640 rokiem. Światło do wnętrza doprowadzały początkowo trzy otwory okienne zdobione witrażami z 1596 roku z przedstawieniami świętych (m.in. śś. Krzysztofa i Pawła), a w 1620 roku pojawiły się jeszcze dwa dodatkowe w prezbiterium (od południa i północy). Nawę i prezbiterium nakrywa wspólny dach, a na styku obu części znajduje się wieża na sygnaturkę z 1653 roku. Około 1910 roku wybudowano wieżę. Remontowany m.in. w 1854 roku i latach 1963–1965 według projektu architekta Lecha Stachowskiego. We wnętrzu zachowała się XVI-wieczna polichromia z przedstawieniem m.in. Drzewa Jessego, a także malowidła Tadeusza Terleckiego z 1930 roku. Świątynia wybudowana w latach 1595–1597, kon se krowana w 1597 roku, jednak gruntownie przebudowana od 1857 do 1858 roku. Budynek orientowany, nawa główna szersza i wyższa od prezbiterium, które zamknięte trójbocznie. Wewnątrz sporo zachowanych elementów pierwotnego wyposażenia, m.in. obraz Święta Trójca z ok. 1600 roku oraz Ukrzyżowanie z adorującymi krzyż fundatorami i podaną datą konsekracji budynku w ołtarzu bocznym z końca XVI wieku. Polichromia z początku XX wieku. Kościół remontowany w latach 1965–1966 i 1996–1998. Zespół kościoła pw. Podwyższenia Krzyża i klasztor Bernardynów Już w chwili sprowadzenia bernardynów do Tarnowa w 1459 roku stał przygotowany dla nich drewniany kościół i klasztor, jednak w 1468 roku ich miejsce zajęły późnogotyckie budynki murowane. Pośród zabudowy dominował jednonawowy z węższym wielobocznie zamkniętym prezbiterium kościół pw. MB Śnieżnej z przylegającym doń trójskrzydłowym klasztorem z wirydarzem pośrodku. Po chwilę obecną przetrwały z tego okresu m.in. fragmenty dawnego wystroju prezbiterium i portal z dawnej wieży kościelnej. Po przeniesieniu w latach osiemdziesiątych XVIII wieku bernardynów do budynków po bernardynkach, dotychczasowy zespół kościelno-klasztorny zakonników uległ znacznym zniszczeniom, m.in. w 1809 i 1814 roku w trakcie pożarów. W latach 1823–1825 zburzono wschodnie i zachodnie skrzydło klasztoru. Pozostałością po pierwotnych zabudowa-

niach bernardyńskich jest budynek przy ul. Bernardyńskiej 19, fragment południowego skrzydła klasztoru, przebudowany w stylu klasycystycznym w 1823 roku. Zachowany do czasów współczesnych klasztor przy ul. Bernardyńskiej 13 powstał w 1680 roku i najpierw stanowił własność bernardynek, które przebywały w Tarnowie od 1555 roku. Klasztor początkowo przylegał do drewnianego kościoła z ok. 1630 roku, w którego miejscu stanął w latach 1752–1776 murowany kościół pw. Podwyższenia Krzyża Świętego, a jego fundatorami byli Paweł i Barbara Sanguszkowie. Korpus jednonawowy z węższym prezbiterium (tak nawa, jak i prezbiterium dwuprzęsłowe) nie leżą dokładnie na jednej osi kościoła, z uwagi na przebieg ulicy. Kościół salowy, doświetlany przez okna od strony południowej, nakryty dachem siodłowym, zróżnicowanym pod względem wysokości. Przy północnej ścianie prezbiterium znajdował się skarbczyk (od 1954 roku kaplica Jezusa Miłosiernego), przy południowej – zakrystia, a do nawy od zachodu przylegało oratorium zakonne (obecnie chór muzyczny). W 1954 roku przeprowadzono remont, w 1960 roku odnowiono polichromię (Karol Pustelnik), w 1980 wykonano żelbetowe schody na chór, a w 1987 roku zamontowano marmurowe posadzki. Teren klasztorny wyznacza murowany i tynkowany parkan, w obręb którego można dostać się bramą (w uskoku parkanu) po zachodniej stronie. Zespół budynków przebudowanych lub powstałych w latach 1877–1931, pomiędzy którymi znajdują się zarówno zabudowania klasztorne, jak i szkolne (ul. Bema 9 i 11), budynek internatu (ul. J. Bema 13; obiekt z 1. połowy XIX wieku, rozbudowany w 1878 i 1898 roku) oraz pozostałości XIX-wiecznego ogrodu, a pośród nich figura NMP Niepokalanie Poczętej z 1880 roku, figura św. Józefa z Dzieciątkiem z 1891 roku oraz fragmenty ogrodzenia i zabudowy gospodarczej z początku XX wieku. W 1877 roku do Tarnowa przybyło 17 zakonnic i zamieszkało w parterowym domu ofiarowanym im przez kanonika Karola Krausa i Marię Wittler (ob. ul. Bema 13). Karol Polityński wybudował w latach 1877–1878 kościół dla sióstr i zaadaptował zakupione nieruchomości na potrzeby zgromadzenia. W 1884 roku z inicjatywy urszulanek wzniesiono zaprojektowaną przez Antoniego Schmitzeka szkołę pw. św. Urszuli (ul. Bema 11). Między 1885 a 1889 rokiem wystawiono dwupiętrowy dom, tzw. klauzurę projektu Schmitzeka, w 1889 roku nadbudowano drugie piętro nieruchomości (obecnie przy ul. Bema 13) według projektu Franciszka Hackbeila i wówczas rozpoczęto rozbudowę zakładu szkolnego (przy ob. ul. Bema 11) według projektu Jana Lewińskiego ze Lwowa. W 1898 roku nadbudowano piętro nad pierwszym domem ofiarowanym urszulankom. W 1903 i 1906 roku powstały budynki gospodarcze i mury, a w 1907 przy budynku szkoły dobudowano dwupiętrowe skrzydło. Na początku lat dwudziestych XX wieku zespół klasztorny składał się z klauzury, kaplicy i dwóch piętrowych budynków szkolnych. W 1924 roku dokończono skrzydło budynku szkolnego (ul. Bema 11), a cały zespół obejmował kaplicę, cztery kamienice i ogród. W 1931 roku wybudowano nowy gmach szkolny według projektu Edwarda Okonia.

Przedstawiciele Zgromadzenia Misjonarzy św. Wincentego à Paulo osiedlili się w Tarnowie w 1904 roku i tymczasowo ich kościołem była drewniana świątynia na Burku. Właściwe zabudowania zespołu kościelno-klasztornego misjonarzy zostały zaprojektowane przez Jana Sas-Zubrzyckiego i wykonane przez budowniczych pod kierunkiem Augusta Tarkowskiego na gruncie ofiarowanym zgromadzeniu przez księcia Eustachego Sanguszkę. Neogotycka świątynia pw. św. Rodziny została wzniesiona w latach 1904–1908 jako budynek murowany na cokole z łupanego piaskowca z Ciężkowic i w wyższych partiach ścian ceglany. Kościół został konsekrowany 4 X 1908 roku przez bp. Leona Wałęgę. Około 1910 roku plac wokół kościoła wyłożono „taflami cementowymi”, wydzielając chodniki. Remontowany po drugiej wojnie światowej, m.in. w związku z uszkodzeniami wojennymi z 1944 roku. Teren przykościelny wyznacza mur z czasów budowy, jednak mocno przebudowany w latach sześćdziesiątych XX wieku, oraz kapliczka przykościelna z pierwszej połowy XIX wieku. Integralną częścią zespołu jest także obecna plebania, a niegdyś klasztor, mieszczący pokoje mieszkalne, refektarz i kuchnię, który przestał pełnić pierwotną funkcję po wybudowaniu w 1976 i 1985 roku nowych dwóch budynków parafialnych. Budynek klasztoru został poświęcony i oficjalnie oddany do użytku 23 V 1908 roku. Kościół pw. Krzyża Świętego i Matki Boskiej Nieustającej Pomocy Wezwanie nawiązuje do pierwotnego patrocinium oraz czczonego w świątyni wizerunku Matki Boskiej Nieustającej Pomocy, przywiezionego w 1914 roku z Rzymu. W miejscu obecnego kościoła stał pierwotnie drewniany krzyż, a następnie wznoszona w latach 1883–1884 niewielka kaplica, stanowiąca wotum za ustanie dotkliwej dla mieszkańców podtarnowskiej wsi Krzyż zarazy w 1873 roku. Projektantem kaplicy był Józef Szebesta. Dnia 21 IX 1884 roku odbyło się uroczyste jej poświęcenie, którego dokonał kanonik tarnowskiej kapituły katedralnej ks. Stanisław Walczyński. Kaplicę rozbudowano w latach 1909–1910 według projektu Augustyna Tarkowskiego, wykonawcą był majster murarski Jan Marek. Powiększony obiekt stał się małym kościołem, przy którym 10 V 1925 roku erygowano osobną parafię pw. św. Krzyża. Po 1945 roku uszkodzone ściany groziły zawaleniem, a wskutek włączenia Krzyża w granice miasta Tarnowa w 1958 roku nastąpił rozwój przestrzenny i demograficzny tej dzielnicy. Nowy kościół powstawał na fundamentach poprzedniego w latach 1968–1971 jako trójnawowa świątynia z wieżą od frontu. Obiekt konsekrowano w 1975 roku. Skwer i bima jako trwała ruina stanowią relikt po istniejącej w tym miejscu do 1941 roku Synagogi zwanej Starą, która została spalona 8 XI 1939 roku, a dwa lata później wysadzona i rozebrana. Początkowo stała w jej miejscu drewniana bożnica z 1582 roku, spełniająca potrzeby niewielkiej populacji żydowskiej w Tarnowie. Najpewniej uległa pożarowi w pierwszych de-

kadach XVII wieku i zastąpiła ją murowana. Ulegała kolejnym pożarom, a na budowę kolejnych uzyskano zgody w 1661 i 1670 roku. Ta ostatnia została rozbudowana w 1796 roku, kiedy pojawił się zachodni przedsionek i północny aneks (spłonęły w 1814 roku). Stanowiła przykład synagogi centralnej. Kolejne rozbudowy przeprowadzono w latach 1815–1848 (wydłużono synagogę w kierunku zachodnim, a także zagospodarowano przestrzeń wokół niej w rodzaj zespołu synagogalnego). W latach siedemdziesiątych–osiemdziesiątych XIX wieku zyskała neoromańską część frontową. Na początku XX stulecia teren wokół synagogi otoczono ogrodzeniem, a w 1929 roku dobudowano do niej drewniany przedsionek. Pozostała po niej bima została w 1987 roku zabezpieczona zadaszeniem i wkomponowana w rozplanowaną przestrzeń upamiętniającą synagogę. Wzniesiony w ostatnich dwóch dekadach XVIII wieku w miejscu drewnianej karczmy Sanguszków. Pierwotnie barokowy „Dom Książęcy” Hieronima Sanguszki był dwuskrzydłowy i trójkondygnacyjny, a jego otoczenie stanowiły m.in. stajnie. Obok kamienicy zwanej „Książęcą” przy rynku w Tarnowie pałac stanowił drugą w mieście budowlę wiązaną z siedzibą Sanguszków. Od 1825 roku zakupiony przez władze państwa budynek zamieniono w siedzibę władz cyrkularnych i następnie powiatu. Obiekt przebudowywano w latach trzydziestych i siedemdziesiątych XIX wieku, a także na przełomie XIX i XX stulecia, dostosowując układ i wygląd obiektu do potrzeb władz cyrkularnych/powiatowych. W czasie tego ostatniego remontu fasadzie nadano formy neobarokowe. Szczęsny Zaremba jako dyrektor budownictwa Tarnowa nadał obiektowi charakter ujednoliconego stylistycznie budynku, wpasowującego się w panujące w monarchii wzorce. Pośród zachowanych po współczesność obiektów o charakterze obronnym, najstarsze są datowane na okres od XIV do XVI stulecia. Po chwilę obecną stanowią je: dwukondygnacyjny późnogotycki ceglano-kamienny półbastion z XVI wieku z zachowanymi strzelnicami półkolistymi rozglifionymi do wewnątrz, ceglana baszta z pierwotnym sklepieniem kopulastym i śladami strzelnic oraz ok. 400 metrów zachowanych fortyfikacji miejskich – murów i przedmurza (w 1959 roku było to zaledwie 15 odcinków), w których konstrukcji dominuje cegła zendrówka, układana w wątkach kowadełkowym lub/i polskim. Na ich podstawie wiadomo, że tarnowskie mury obronne tworzyły nieregularny owal, dostosowany do topografii terenu obecnej Starówki. W latach 1648–1651 obwarowania były poddane gruntownemu remontowi, a jedne z ostatnich prac wzmiankowano w latach osiemdziesiątych XVII wieku, kiedy to fortyfikacje były już przestarzałe i nie spełniały swojej podstawowej funkcji. Od ostatniej dekady XVIII do początku XIX wieku likwidowano tarnowskie umocnienia, a ich pozostałości opisywano w 1959 roku jako ruiny. Ich stan zaczął się poprawiać w latach 1961– 1965, kiedy to zostały zabezpieczone i wyeksponowane w latach 1954–1969.

Park został założony w miejscu dawnego miejskiego folwarku Podwale Dyksonówka. Projekt ogrodnika z Krosna – Antoniego Schmidta realizowano od 1866 roku, dzieląc przestrzeń na część spacerową i gospodarczą (od zachodu podzieloną jeszcze na szkółkę drzew i ogród warzywny). Integralną przestrzenią jest także strzelnica Towarzystwa Strzeleckiego i jej otoczenie (południowo-zachodnia część parku, wykończenie wnętrz proj. Janusza Rypuszyńskiego z 1891 roku). Nieodzownym elementem parku były lub są nadal: neogotycka strzelnica (ok. 1866), oranżeria (ok. 1894, przebudowana w 1929, 1936 i 1955), cieplarnia (1878), dwukomnatowy domek i drewniana budka dla stróża (ok. 1873, zastąpił ją budynek bramny dla stróża), dom dla ogrodnika w stylu secesji wiedeńskiej (1902–1907, proj. Szczęsnego Zaremby, w miejscu wcześniejszego z 1894 roku), wodotrysk (1912), mauzoleum (1928), kurant wodny z wiedeńskiej firmy J. A. Hilperta. W 1912 roku zmieniono lokalizację wejścia głównego, przekształcając układ przestrzenny, m.in. zaprowadzając grupowo-smugowy typ zadrzewienia. W latach 1927–1928 zmieniono układ i wygląd parku, dostosowując do funkcji mauzoleum gen. Józefa Bema (projektu Adolfa Szyszko-Bohusza). W 1927 roku otoczono całość betonowym ogrodzeniem z reprezentacyjną bramą wejściową (proj. secesyjnego okucia E. Okoń). Po drugiej wojnie światowej wyasfaltowano uliczki, w 1955 roku zamontowano oświetlenie elektryczne, remontowano budynki oranżerii i zaadaptowano budynki na cele socjalne. Początkowo budynek miał nosić nazwę Hotelu Polskiego, jednak stał się siedzibą Hotelu Bristol rodziny Rypuszyńskich. Obiekt był wznoszony w latach 1904–1906 według projektu Janusza Rypuszyńskiego. Zastosowano w nim rozwiązania typowe dla wczesnego stylu tego architekta, który odwoływał się do secesji i geometrycznych form. W wyniku kształtu działki obiekt ma charakterystyczny układ i plan. Rozbudowany w latach trzydziestych XX wieku, kiedy zmieniono m.in. elewację od ul. Krakowskiej według projektu Witolda Giżbert-Studnickiego, zyskując kosztem dekoracji secesyjnej eklektyczną. Kolejne przebudowy przeprowadzono w latach 1941–1942 (adaptacja na hotel dla Niemców) według projektu biura A. Seiferta i M. Elckmayera. W latach 1949–1962 prowadzono prace adaptacyjno-modernizacyjne. Budynek został wzniesiony według projektu Karola Polityńskiego w latach 1880–1882 jako siedziba tarnowskiej Kasy Oszczędności (na parterze) oraz Towarzystw – Kasynowe- go i Muzycznego (piętro). W 1896 roku nastąpiła rozbudowa obiektu według projektu Adolfa Stapfa, kiedy m.in. wydłużono jedno ze skrzydeł i zmieniono układ przestrzenny obiektu. W 1929 roku zastąpiono drewnianą konstrukcję głównej klatki schodowej żelazobetonową, dopasowując ją do potrzeb budynku spełniającego zarówno funkcje kasowe, jak i kulturalne. W 1949 roku dokonano remontu lokalu na potrzeby PZPR, wprowadzając nowe ściany działowe i wymieniając terakotowe posadzki na parkiety. Wówczas też malowano ściany wewnątrz budynku. W 1964 roku dokonano renowacji Sali Lustrzanej, a w latach 2011–2013 przeprowadzono konserwację dekoracji wnętrz – sztukaterii, kamieniarki i stolarki okiennej.

Parterowy dwutraktowy drewniany dwór w całości podpiwniczony i nakryty czterospadowym wysokim dachem łamanym tzw. polskim był wzmiankowany już pod koniec XVIII wieku. Z czasem ściany zmieniono na murowane. Stanowi świadectwo dawnej zabudowy Przedmieścia Krakowskiego, którą tworzyły m.in. zajazd Sanguszków z 1799 roku (w miejscu dawnej karczmy Rhodów za Bramą Krakowską; po przebudowach Hotel Krakowski) i gmach poczty ze stacją dyliżansów. Od 1903 roku stanowi własność miasta, w 1927 roku zorganizowano w nim muzeum miejskie. Gruntownie odremontowany w latach siedemdziesiatych XX wieku. Jego otoczenie stanowi ogród i drewniany spichlerz z końca XVIII wieku. Klasycystyczny dworek wzniesiono na początku XIX wieku jako obiekt drewniany, dwutraktowy i jednopiętowy. Od strony fasady znajduje się czterokolumnowy portyk. Z czasem do elewacji północnej dostawiono murowaną przybudówkę z amfiladowym układem pomieszczeń. W latach trzydziestych XX wieku drewniane ściany zmieniono na murowane. W 1959 roku budynek uznano za silnie uszkodzony, jednak podjęto prace naprawcze i w 1966 roku sklasyfikowano go jako częściowo uszkodzony. Obiekt został sprzedany w 1975 roku na rzecz Skarbu Państwa. Pod koniec lat siedemdziesiątych XX wieku wykonano nowe ogrodzenie. Klasycystyczny budynek z pierwszej połowy XIX wieku w charakterze podmiejskiej rezydencji. Mieszkała w nim rodzina Kostasiów, m.in. majordomus Eustachego Sanguszki – Tadeusz Kostaś, który otrzymał od księcia Eustachego na własność tę nieruchomość. Generalny remont będącego ruiną dworu przeprowadzono w latach 2018–2020, zamieniając obiekt w przestrzeń restauracyjną. The first people appeared in the area of the future town and its surroundings around 11,000 years ago. They were groups of reindeer hunters who lived from hunting these animals in the glacier foreland, in a climate similar to the tundra. Most of the finds from this period were made by the amateur archaeologist Boleslaw Czapkiewicz1, who found a number of flint tools belonging to the so-called Mazowiecki Cycle of the late Palaeolithic – arrowheads, knives, scrapers, and flint piercers – south of the Piaskówka district. The warming of the following millennia caused the reindeer herds to move northwards, and groups of reindeer hunters followed. The area of today’s Tarnów was covered with forests, and a hunter-gatherer population appeared, depending for their sustenance on the fruits and game found in the forests. Flint tools were microlithised, with small arrow microliths being the most common. In the area of Tarnów, there are six archaeological sites from the Mesolithic period, most of which, unfortunately, have not been precisely located, except for the statement ‘south of Piaskówka, between Rzędzin and Tarnów.’ These sites, located on sand dunes, have probably been destroyed or built over as a consequence of human activity.

Around the middle of the 5th millennium BC, groups of people from the south began to arrive in Poland, bringing with them the skills of cultivation and agriculture, and one of the greatest revolutions in human history, the so-called Neolithic Revolution, took place. The nomadic lifestyle of hunters and gatherers gave way to a sedentary way of life, and the first permanent settlements and burial grounds appeared. The process of settling southern Poland by farmers unfolded over several centuries. The fertile loess areas around Kraków and Miechów were the first to be occupied, and it was from these regions that the initial farmers emerged near Tarnów. Between 4300 and 4200 BC, Neolithic groups began migrating eastward towards the vicinity of Rzeszów and Przeworsk. 1 Bolesław Czapkiewicz (1873–1942), painter, teacher, archaeologist. He was the first to conduct archaeological explorations in Tarnów and excavations within the city and in the forks of the Wątok and Biała Dunajcowa rivers. In his search for prehistoric settlement, he traversed the southern part of Tarnów, Zawada, Krzyż, and Wola Rzędzińska. The results of his research covered a wide spectrum of prehistory from the Stone Age to the Roman influence period. The areas he explored are now completely built-up and archaeologically degraded. Traces within the city limits suggest a brief presence of the Linear Pottery culture population, with only a few flint tools from this culture discovered in the inventories documented by Czapkiewicz. The examination of flint tools uncovered by Czapkiewicz also reveals evidence of another Neolithic culture in the city area – the Lengyel culture. The flint tools associated with the Lengyel culture originate from the areas of Rzędzin and Grabówka. No traces of settlements from the initial farmers have been found. Only between St. Martin’s Hill (Góra św. Marcina) and the town did B. Czapkiewicz identify traces of a Neolithic camp. It appears that, during this period, the lands north of the Carpathian foothills in our region were primarily explored by Neolithic cultures for economic purposes rather than serving as permanent settlements. Consequently, we can only document isolated finds from the Neolithic period, such as a blade discovered during the archaeological exploration of townhouse no. 5 in Rynek or an arrowhead found in the allotment gardens along the river Wątok. At the end of the Neolithic period (3rd millennium BC), another wave of people associated with the so-called Corded Ware Culture (CWC) left traces in the city’s area. The people of this culture were pastoralists, and their deceased were interred beneath burial mounds. Often, the only remaining evidence of these mounds is represented by discoveries of stone axes and hatchets placed in the graves of the dead. A total of four hatchets and seven stone axes associated with this culture have been unearthed within the city limits.

The date 1800 BC marks the conventional boundary between the Neolithic and the beginning of the Bronze Age in Poland. During this transitional period, the first copper objects emerged. Copper rings discovered in our region may be a trace of a trade route along the Dunajec river valley from south to north, from the area of present-day Romania, where copper was mined already in prehistoric times. Research in the 1980s unveiled two archaeological cultures from the Early Bronze Age in the vicinity of Tarnów. The first is the Mierzanowice culture, which existed in our area until about 1600 BC. Traces of a hut associated with this culture were unearthed at site no. 1 in Tarnowiec, in the immediate vicinity of the city limits, while site no. 5, situated on the opposite side of the river Biała in Koszyce Wielkie, yielded isolated finds. The Koszyce site also revealed a pair of richly decorated bronze bracelets. The widespread use of bronze is connected to the extensive archaeological culture that thrived in our region for nearly 1,000 years – the Lusatian culture. Traces of several settlements of this culture have been discovered to the south of the compact development of the city. It is likely that already in the new era, the Iron Age, the inhabitants of these settlements buried their dead on the sandy hill on which the Old Town of Tarnów was later built. Fragments of a vase, indicating a burial, were discovered in the cellars of the Town Hall, while an urn grave found behind the townhouse at Rynek 5 confirmed this hypothesis. As part of rescue excavations along the urban bypass, excavations were carried out at Site no. 7, revealing traces of a settlement from the Lusatian culture. Additional traces of a settlement from this culture were discovered on the opposite bank of a small stream in Tarnowiec, at Site no. 1, as well as at Site no. 88 in Tarnów. The hillfort in Zawada, under investigation since 1982, provided information that during the Lusatian culture, or more precisely its late phase, a defensive gord, similar to the previously known hillfort in Zawada Lanckorońska existed there. The existence of the hillfort as an administrative or tribal centre confirms earlier information about the dense settlement of the discussed culture in the southern part of the city, with the river Biała serving as the axis of this settlement cluster.

Changes in human settlement underway gave rise to the emergence of village-like settlements and an increase in population density, primarily along rivers. Spiritual culture was evolving, and the custom of cremating the deceased, associated with the sun cult, became widespread. New agricultural techniques, the development of crafts and bronze metallurgy stabilised the economic foundations of human communities. In 1873, a bronze sword with a hilt of the so-called antenna type was found on the dunes near Tarnów – an example of either local craftsmanship or far-reaching trade contacts. Another artefact indicating ancient metallurgy is the discovery of a decorated bronze ring – a fragment of a necklace. Excavations in the marketplace known as Burek uncovered a cremation grave of the Pomeranian culture. This culture succeeded the Lusatian culture. The decline of the Lusatian culture and the new cultural trends associated with the significant expansion of the Celtic peoples over large areas of Europe led to the emergence of the Przeworsk culture in the 2nd and 1st centuries BC. This culture continued also into the period of Roman influence, from the 1st to the 4th century AD. A cremation grave from the socalled Tyniec group (2nd–1st century BC), discovered in 1996, is evidence of the penetration of the Celtic-Przeworsk population into the Tarnów region. The duration of the Przeworsk culture is a well-recognised archaeological period. Boleslaw Czapkiewicz, who researched a settlement from the later phase of the Roman influence, is worth mentioning here once again. We know of several dozen archaeological sites from this period in the city. Excavations at several sites close to the city limits have provided extensive data on the chronology of settlements of this culture, the lifestyle of the inhabitants and burial rituals due to the investigated cemetery at Łętowice, near Tarnów, where over 30 cremation graves were discovered, richly equipped with various everyday objects, vessels, and weapons. The number of finds is so extensive that it has been possible to delineate the Tarnów cluster on the map of settlements in the Dunajec valley during that period. This cluster comprises numerous settlements situated to the south of the city and in the areas of Koszyce Wielkie, Nowodworze, and Tarnowiec. In the latter, near the city limits, a settlement of the Przeworsk culture was excavated (research by J. Okoński and A. Szpunar), covering several hectares of land, with a distinct residential zone (about a dozen houses) and a production zone (several hundred hearths). In addition to traces of settlements, objects from the Roman Empire have also been discovered, such as coins found in brickworks near St. Martin’s Hill (Góra Marcina), where a denarius of Vespasian and a gold solidus of Theodosius were unearthed.

The Przeworsk culture faded away, and following the migration of peoples, materials associated with the Slavs appeared in the town. There are no traces of early Slavic culture (5th–6th centuries); most of the finds date back to the 9th–11th centuries. From this period onwards, we can speak of ethnic-cultural continuity in the area of Tarnów and its surroundings. Among more than twenty archaeological sites related to this period, the most significant include the Gord in Zawada, partially located within the city limits (Tarnów Site no. 101), the excavated early medieval settlement in Klikowa, and isolated finds of early medieval pottery from the area of the Old Town. There are no clear traces of an early medieval settlement on the hill where Tarnów is situated. Extensive research along the A4 motorway has provided the answer to a question that has puzzled archaeologists for years: where did the people who built the massive settlement at Zawada live? In the axis of the Dunajec Valley, entire villages were discovered, with dozens of houses, hearths, and complete homesteads (Wierzchosławice, Sites nos. 11 and 12, 15, Gosławice, Site no. 5, Komorów, Site no. 8) The town of Tarnów was located on a small elevation (226 m above sea level) in the valley of the river Biała, on the border between the Sandomierz Basin and the Carpathian Foothills, in a predominantly forested area, although partly affected by earlier settlement activity. The location of the town was influenced by the stream Wątok, which flowed south of Tarnów, and the now non-existent stream Strusina (Trosina), which flowed parallel to the Wątok from the fields of Rzędzin and Wola Rzędzińska to the river Biała. Trade routes connecting the Baltic Sea with Hungary ran through the valley of the river Biała and the nearby river Dunajec, intersecting near Tarnów with the route leading to Ruthenia.2 The charter was issued in Krakow on 7 March 1330 by Władysław Łokietek at the request of Spicymir, the voivode of Kraków. The monarch transferred the villages of Tarnów Wielki and Tarnów Mały from the Środa law to Magdeburg law and also consented to the establishment of a town on their territory, with a system modelled on that of Kraków.3 Tarnów Mały comprised the area of the modern-day villages of Tarnowiec and Zawada to the south of the town, with the centre of the settlement in the area of today’s. The church there is considered the oldest in the area.4 The town itself was founded on the territory of the village of Tarnów Wielki, whose name was transferred to the urban centre.5 It is not known whether Spicymir

Crucial to the reconstruction of the settlement programme of a medieval town is the determination of the size of the settlement lot. It is usually determined on the basis of statistical studies of the width measurements of preserved contemporary lots. However, the results of lot width measurements in Tarnów are inconclusive. They indicate a slight concentration around the value of 14–14.5 m, which, using the size of the Kraków foot (Tarnów was chartered on the model of Kraków), gives a size close to 47–50 ft.10 However, there is no mediaeval material available to verify this measurement. Besides a few isolated relics, no traces of burgher architecture from before the 16th century have survived in Tarnów. The first surviving inventories of income from burgher property date only from the 17th century, and therefore, research should be based on them.11 We have three such inventories – one for the northern part from 1618 and two for the southern part: undated but probably from the early 1650s and 1675.12 They all show the annual rent collected in the town and paid from the rooftop.13 A list of the houses in Tarnów, included in the deed of division of the Ostrogski estate in 1603, also gives a lot of information about the spatial layout.14 Between 1603 and 1618, the northern frontage of the market of Monuments, Tarnów Branch (hereinafter: AWUOZ), inventory no. 2774 I, Tarnów. On this basis, it can be hypothesised that the western part of the town was intended to be laid out in the same way as the eastern part. What prevented this was the topography, in the form of a steep escarpment. When the town walls were later built, they were placed along the edge of the escarpment, and the urban development followed the course of the wall. The original purpose of the southern part of today’s Plac Katedralny is also unclear. Some authors consider Plac Katedralny a lot of land allocated to the church at the time of the town’s foundation.28 Archaeological research in Plac Katedralny has revealed a number of late medieval and early modern burials, which seems to confirm the early religious character of this part of the square as well.29 Modern sources, however, indicate that the southern part of the square was occupied by burgher buildings by the end of the 16th century at the latest and was given to the church only in the 17th century, to be demolished at the turn of the 18th and 19th centuries.30 The site for the church was located outside the basic chartered layout of the town, at the highest point of the elevation, with the northwestern block of the town lots. Originally, the town was accessed through two gates: Krakowska in the west and Pilzneńska in the east. The exact location of the Krakowska Gate is not known, but it is believed to have been located along today’s ul. Katedralna or south of it, within the premises of the present building at ul. Katedralna 4.41 According to a late report (1732), in addition to the main entrance, there were two side entrances for pedestrians.42 The Pilzneńska Gate, on the other hand, stood in the course of today’s ul. Pilzneńska. It was housed in a massive rectangular tower measuring approximately 7.5 by 8 metres. The width of the entrance was 2.4 metres.43 Living quarters were located on the first floor.44 The connecting wall, built of brick on a foundation of fieldstone and broken stone, was between 1.5 and 2 metres thick.45 The Minor Gate (Porta Minori) is mentioned in a list of guild representatives responsible for preventing theft in the event of a fire in 1557 and can be identified as the wicket at the exit of today’s ul. Wielkie Schody.46 According to some authors, this entrance was rebuilt as a gate in the second half of the 16th century, but the constant use of the name furtka (wicket) to refer to it and the layout of the land seem to contradict this.47 The gate in today’s ul. The parish church in Tarnów was erected shortly after the town’s foundation and the arrival of settlers. However, the first documented information about it dates back to 1346.53 Around the turn of the 14th and 15th centuries, the church underwent expansion or perhaps a complete reconstruction, this time as a brick structure. The limited information that has survived attests to the undertaken works. In 1399, a Tarnów burgher named Kuńcza endowed the altar of St. Bartholomew, and approximately in 1400, the Chapel of Corpus Christi (Holy Cross) was founded. The document confirming this foundation mentions the existence of a chancel.54 In 1400, the Tarnów church was elevated to the status of a collegiate church.55 Three prelatures (prebendary, custodian, and cantor) and two prebendary canonries (of St. Mary in the Castle and St. Bartholomew) were established. It is connected with the Provost Marcin Łyczko, who acted in agreement with the Hetman Jan Tarnowski, the school’s patron.82 In 1597, the school was the largest building in the chapter complex, with a large study hall and living quarters for the rector, cantor, and pupils.83 It is likely that during the construction of the brick building, the house of the deceased citizen Stanisław Bałachowski, bought by the then rector Paweł Łącki in 1559, situated on the other side of the wall in the street next to the house of the furrier Walenty, was incorporated into the building.84 The canons of Tarnów did not attach much importance to the ownership of the houses they occupied, settling wherever living space was available.85 Therefore, no special significance should be attached to the names of the subsequent houses. What is important, however, is that in the period from the early 15th to the end of the 16th century, a dense series of chapter houses were built around the church, on its east and north sides, from the rector’s house and school to the chancellor’s house. Sources indicate that these were small buildings, usually consisting of a corridor and a room on the ground floor and one or more small rooms on the upper floor. These houses were destroyed by normal wear-and-tear or by the fires that ravaged the town. They were often rebuilt in a form different from the original. Nevertheless, they were a relatively permanent element of the urban layout of the town. As already mentioned, the centre of the town was occupied by a market square, where a series of administrative and commercial buildings was erected in the 14th and 15th centuries, the most prominent of which is the Town Hall (the only surviving building). According to the most recent findings, this building was erected at the end of the 15th century on the site of an earlier wooden structure mentioned in 1448.86 All that remains of the earlier phase is a dry well located under the northern wall of the building.87 In the second half of the 16th century and

The Jews were to draw water from this source, bearing 2/3 of the costs of its maintenance.125 In the Middle Ages, Tarnów was dominated by timber development and thus was prone to destruction by fire. It was only in the 16th century that most of the houses, at least in the front part, were built of brick. The literature associates the reconstruction of Tarnów with the efforts of Hetman Jan Tarnowski, although it appears to have commenced earlier, following the fires of 1483 and 1494.126 Nonetheless, Hetman Tarnowski undoubtedly made numerous successful endeavours to develop the towns under his ownership, including Tarnów. These efforts manifested in a series of privileges granted to guilds and regulations for the inhabitants of Tarnów, which were issued in 1554–1560 and regulated various aspects of life in the town.127 Two of these regulations are worth mentioning: one for bricklayers, carpenters, and stonemasons (1554) and a general one from around 1556.128 In the first one, Tarnowski, among other things, reserved the right to approve, personally or through his official, the location, size, and height of houses to be built in Tarnów. He prohibited the occupation of street space for construction without his consent and mandated the construction of a new house for the organist and other church servants.129 In the second, entitled Nauka a porządek około gaszenia ognia... (Science and Order Concerning Firefighting…), he introduced the division of the town into quarters (wiertle), at the head of each of which he appointed a wiertelnik (a reeve) elected by the townspeople, and the inhabitants assigned to them were obligated to extinguish fires.130 Tarnowski also mandated the appointment of burghers responsible for preventing thefts during 125 ...A canal called Fontana from which a Jew Lazarowicz drew water to his house in 1645 MTH (as n. 17), no. 229. A canal from which Jews drew water to the detriment of the town well is also attested in 1636 MTH (as n. 17), no. 134. F. Herzig, Tarnów (as n. 40), p. 120. A water supply system carrying water from the vicinity of the boundary with Krzyż and Pogwizdów is shown on Grottger’s plan from 1797. It runs through the fields to the well on the canon grange, then to the well in today’s ul. Rybna, from where it goes through today’s ul. Piekarska to the market square, to the well on the south-west side of the Town Hall and through ul. Wielkie Schody outside the town ANK (as n. 12), ref. no. 663.963.

Bidwell- neighbours were the apothecary Stanisław Zawicki and his stepmother Jadwiga, who occupied one room and a ‘sklep’ (a room with a brick vault) for life.142 The most magnificent building in the northern frontage was undoubtedly the townhouse of Jakub Wąs. It was built in the second half of the 16th century by Jakub Wąs, a wealthy merchant and mayor who also owned two suburban houses and a brewery.143 The Wąs townhouse was a brick building with a cellar and an upper floor, with stables and a brewery at the back. On the ground floor, there was an arcade, a vaulted porch and a chamber, another chamber with three wooden walls and one brick wall heated by a tiled stove, side rooms, a kitchen and a kitchen storeroom under the brick staircase leading to the first floor. On the first floor, there was a chamber, two rooms with windows, and a veranda overlooking the square. From the first floor, a wooden staircase led to the attic, which was closed by a door.144 The interiors were decorated with paintings, some of which have been preserved to this day.145 The Erazmusowska townhouse, belonging to Sebastian Miecznik, was equally impressive.146 According to the description from 1605, it had a cellar, a large vaulted room on the ground floor, a smaller vaulted room next to it, a large hall above the larger vaulted room on the first floor, and a small room with a chamber and another room above it.147 Jerzy Sroth, a councillor, had his house behind the Erazmusowska townhouse.148 The results of the architectural study of the present state of the building suggest that at the beginning of the 17th century, it could have been a two-aisled, one-storey brick building with an arcade, similar in height and construction to the Erazmusowska house.149

The western frontage comprised five townhouses, starting with the house of Jan Stania, a tinsmith, and ending with the Red House, which already belonged to the second section.150 Jan Stania’s house, built at the end of the 16th century, was a brick building with arcades and an upper floor. It occupied the front part of the lot, featuring two vaulted rooms on the ground floor separated by a long, narrow corridor.151 To the south, Jan Stania’s house was adjacent to the Kochanowska house, owned by Walenty Kochan, wójt (mayor) of Tarnów.152 Built in the second half of the 16th century, it covered the entire width of the lot. The ground floor boasted a large vaulted hall leading to two smaller side rooms, also vaulted. A brick staircase from the hall led to five or six rooms on the first floor, also vaulted, with a portico at the front.153 Behind the Kochan’s house stood the houses of Melchior Ćwikliński and Jerzy Eneasz Schot.154 Jerzy Eneasz, or Ennis Schot, an Edinburgh-born merchant, settled permanently in Tarnów at the end of the 16th century when he bought a townhouse in Rynek from Marcin Koziowolski.155 The Red House, named after Marcin the Red, its 16th-century owner, stood at the very end of this frontage.156 In the second half of the 17th century, its owner was Jakub Ćwikłowski.157 In 1603, at the western edge of the southern frontage stood the property of Wojciech Anioł, wójt (mayor) of Tarnów.158 Until 1600, his neighbour to the east was Jan Kostek, a barbersurgeon, and later his daughter Agnieszka, who married Sebastian Łękawski.159 The reason remains unknown, but in 1600, the Kestczyna townhouse, also known as the Maltisek house, was destroyed.160 Consequently, its owner relinquished her ownership rights, ultimately selling the house in 1604 to Wawrzyniec Tribak and his wife, Jadwiga.161 On the eastern side of the Kostek house stood the townhouse of Wojciech Król (Królik).162 This Tarnów merchant acquired it from Marcin Ćwikliński in -Hołdys, Kupcy w siedemnastowiecznym Tarnowie, [in:] “Śląski Kwartalnik Historyczny – Sobótka” 30 (1975) 2, p. 228. 142 ANK (as n. 12), ref. no. 637.3038, p. 32. In the second half of the 16th century, Scots began to settle in Tarnów, likely at the invitation of Duke Konstantin Ostrogski.216 Unlike the Jewish community, the Scots, whether Catholic or Protestant, quickly assimilated into Polish culture despite resistance from the local population. They acquired houses in the town and assumed municipal roles through purchases or marital relations. At the beginning of the 17th century, besides the already well-known George Eneas Schot, the sources mention others, including Piotr Bernard and Tomasz Szot, Jakub and Andrzej Ross, Aleksander Duf, and Peterson Kilian—father of Bałka Kilian, wójt (mayor) of Tarnów and a benefactor of the Scapular Brotherhood chapel in the Tarnów church.217 By the mid-17th century, around fifteen Scottish families resided in Tarnów, mainly involved in trade and, to a lesser extent, craftsmanship.218 Unlike the Jewish community, the Scots did not form a compact settlement, residing both near the market square and in streets branching off from it. While some remained Protestant, they did not establish their own temple. It was only in the early 17th century that an Evangelical Protestant cemetery was established in the Nikielsons’ garden in Przedmieście Wielkie.219 In the first half of the 18th century, the Scottish population in Tarnow became invisible. However, their memory persisted in the names of certain houses, such as Huysnowska, Wilkinsonowska, Nikielesonowska, and Rossowska townhouses in the market square.220 The town in the 2nd half of the 17th century and at the beginning of the 18th century The second half of the 17th century is considered a period of the decline of the town.221 In particular, the Swedish ‘deluge’ is said to have led to significant depopulation and the loss of Tarnów’s economic importance. As can be seen, despite the general crisis of Polish towns in the second half of the 17th century, Tarnów remained an active centre of crafts and trade. There was a steady influx of people willing to settle there. The period of the town’s decline is marked only by the years 1702–1743. During this period, the town was devastated by fires (1702, 1704, 1705, 1708, 1711, 1732, 1735, 1743). In 1705, Tarnów was hit by the plague. It can be assumed that in the 17th century the population of the suburbs made up about 40% of the total population (excluding the village of Pogwizdów, inhabited by about 100–150 people). The moderate population growth in Tarnów lasted until the beginning of the 18th century. It was influenced, on the one hand, by extraordinary losses caused by plagues, fires, and the emigration of inhabitants to other towns and, on the other hand, by the influx of a nonnative population originating from both outlying villages and other towns, mainly from Małopolska (Lesser Poland). As late as 1707, 197 hearths were documented in Tarnów.259 In the first half of the 18th century, however, the town succumbed to a series of misfortunes. As a result, in spite of a continuous influx of population, as can be seen from the book of admissions to the municipal privileges, the census of 1717 puts the number of inhabitants at 644–972, and in 1757, only 82 out of a total of 130 lots were developed, which meant that 656–984 people (excluding the clergy) lived within the town walls.260 From the middle of the 18th century, however, there was a renewed demographic growth due to the influx of population into the rebuilding city. In 1785, Tarnów, together with the suburbs of Zamieście, Burek, and Pogwizdów, had a total population of 3,249, of whom 1,881 were Catholics. In the town itself, there were 109 Catholic families (391 persons) and 266 Jewish families (1,236 persons), a total of 1,627 inhabitants.261 By the end of the 18th century, the population of the town and its suburbs had increased to 3,508262.

Tax registers from the 16th-century document taxes collected from three Tarnów suburbs: suburbium pars prima versus Klikowa, ... pars secunda versus castrum, and, in place of Grabówka, which is listed alongside other villages of the Tarnów parish, suburbium pars tertia versus Zablocie.266 The suburb had 16 lans (lanei agriocolarum) on the castle side and 15 on the Klikowa side. The smallest suburb was Zabłocie, with five lans (lanei agriocolarum), two of which belonged to the Tarnowski grange before 1546.267 While the identification of the fields towards Klikowa seems obvious (this is the northern part of the 19th-century village of Strusina), the location of the fields on the castle side needs to be revised.268 Considering the relative positions of the town and the castle of Tarnów, the area covered by the 19th-century cadastral communes of Zabłocie and Terlikówka lies between them. Terlikówka, as the name of a separate settlement unit, appears only in the middle of the 17th century, referring to the farmsteads located on the road from the town to the castle.269 It can be assumed that the settlement of Przedmieście Wielkie stretched much further to the southeast than the 19th-century administrative divisions indicate. On the northern side of the town, behind the ramparts surrounding it, stretched fields that belonged partly to the Tarnów clergy and partly to the burghers, extending all the way to the village boundary. Starting from the west, there was the curates’ grange, in their hands since 1458, the cantor’s grange, documented as late as 1597. In the 1570s, the parson’s grange on the border with Pogwizdów was mentioned.270 The inventory There is no doubt that as early as the 14th century, a suburban settlement began to develop around Tarnów, partly as a continuation of the pre-charter settlement of the former village of Tarnów Wielki.263 At the beginning of the 15th century, the name suburb was used for it. The first to develop was Przedmieście Wielkie (Great Suburb) on the western side of the city. In 1425, it became necessary to demarcate the boundary between it and the developing neighbouring village of Chyszów.264 In the 1470s, there were 28 lans (lanei agriocolarum) in Przedmieście Wielkie (Górne). Conversely, on the eastern side of the town, Przedmieście Mniejsze or Dolne (Small or Lower Suburb), also known as Grabówka was established, comprising 15 lans (lanei agriocolarum) and one rod owned by the peasants.265

The former included the peasant lans under the jurisdiction of the Tarnów castle, mainly in Przedmieście Wielkie (the Great Suburb), fourteen lans in the direction of the castle and thirteen in the direction of Klikowa, inhabited by about 48 peasants, not counting the tenant farmers who also owned land in Ruda or Wola on the river Biała, granted by the lords

In late May and early June 1772, two groups of Austrian troops crossed the southern borders of the Polish-Lithuan. The first, under the command of Field Marshal Esterházy, entered from northern Hungary (now Slovakia). Its mission was to take Lviv from the Russians. Initially, it was the seat of a district within the Pilzno Circulus.299 In March 1782, the first important decision of the partitioning authorities concerning Tarnów was to establish the seat of a large circulus,300 which in the first period of its existence had a population of over 188,000 (according to the data of 1790).301 This decision stimulated the town’s development, which was all the more important as in the 1890s, during the reign of Emperor Francis II of Habsburg, the Austrians revised the status of towns in Galicia. The firmly established political and administrative position of Tarnów among the towns of Galicia, reinforced in part by Emperor Francis II’s decision, its excellent transportation links, and its economic development, contributed to the particularly favourable demographic growth in the town during the first decades of Austrian rule. The population of Tarnów steadily grew. In 1777, Tarnów, excluding its suburbs, had 117 inhabited houses with only 995 residents. Including the suburbs, the total population was 2,428. Alongside the economic and demographic development of Tarnów, its cultural urbanisation advanced, with the result particularly visible in education. The central part of the town was a quadrangular market square (Rynek) with a town hall in the middle. In the first decades of the 19th century, next to the town hall to the north, there was an infantry guardhouse and the Austrian police headquarters. On the opposite side, to the south, was the jail, the town’s scales, and the fire equipment store – a room considered the original seat of the fire brigade. The upper floors of the town hall housed the town cash office, the magistrate’s offices, and storerooms. After a bull of Pope Leo XII made Tarnów the seat of the diocese in April 1826, the consistory of the diocese was located at Rynek. It was located in a townhouse previously purchased from the Sanguszko family of Gumniska. On the northern frontage of Rynek, there was a pharmacy. The entire frontage was then called pocienie due to the several townhouses connected to each other and their brick arcades. Along this frontage, there were several shops, among which the Tarnów bakeries dominated.319 To the west of the square was a separate square next to the cathedral. Surrounding the square and the church were a number of houses which, at the turn of the 18th and 19th centuries, served as school buildings for the local gymnasium and normal schools. There were also the apartments of the prefect of the gymnasium and the headmaster. Near the cathedral square, to the east, were the municipal stalls. Behind the church was Krakowskie Przedmieście, described on Austrian maps as the Krakauer Vorstadt, in the first half of the 19th century considered the most beautiful part of the city. This area featured a banqueting hall built in 1799. Nearby, there was an inn, renovated in 1828, on the side of the new road whose construction was completed in 1817. The most prominent buildings in this Przedmieście surrounding Plac Pocztowy were the Post Office building (then known as the Post House) and the Fürst Haus (Duke’s House), located opposite on the southern side – a palace, which still served as a residence in the 18th century. In the early years of Austrian rule in Tarnów, the palace was bought by the government and used as the circular office and residence of the Kreishauptmann. The Plac Pocztowy mentioned above was renamed Plac Jana III Sobieskiego in 1883 on the bicentenary of the victory of Vienna.

The aesthetics of the city in the first decades of Austrian rule deserve a little more attention. Austrian travellers visiting the city during that period held divergent views on that matter and provided interesting opinions on the subject. Charles Boromeus Feyerabend, who spent a short time in the city in 1798, described it as ‘not very grand, but neat...’ The German writer was particularly impressed by Tarnów’s Rynek, which was then undergoing extensive renovation.337 A doctor from Vienna, Joseph August Schultes, who came to Tarnów in 1806, was equally impressed. He paid particular attention to Krakowskie Przedmieście, which was then the showpiece of the city. In the letters he penned, he wrote: Upon arriving in Tarnów from Kraków, one gets the impression of being in a German town. Everything looks tidy. The houses are beautiful and clean – good taste and order reign everywhere, but what a contrast to the view of the city centre. And yet, Tarnów is the capital of the region! The road leading from Tarnów to Pilzno, and especially to Dębica, is the most captivating in the whole area between Krakow and Lviv. One might almost feel transported to another country, looking at the well­cultivated fields and well­tended forests.338 331 M. K. Trusz, Burek, (as n. 327), p. 75. 332 Tarnów. Decisions taken on 8 January 1845 were decisive for the spatial development of Tarnów during the Habsburg period. On that memorable day, the authorities of Tarnów signed an agreement with Duke Władysław Sanguszko, by which he relinquished sovereignty over the inhabitants of several neighbouring villages: Grabówka, Strusina, and Zabłocie with Terlikówka. Until then, Zabłocie and Terlikówka formed a single unit with Gumniska, i.e. with the Sanguszko family’s nest. The same was true for Grabówka but from the northwest. It is noteworthy that according to a plan of Tarnów found in the records of the Austrian State Archives in Vienna, drawn up in August 1856 and later printed by the Viennese printing house of Ernest Becher, Terlikówka is referred to by the unused name of Terlinkowa.342 After 1845, the previously mentioned villages were incorporated into Tarnów as suburbs, forming a unified political commune with the town.343 Besides the administrative and spatial changes, the agreement also entailed Sanguszko’s sale to the town of the exclusive right to produce and distribute vodka within the town and the suburb of Zawale, along with the rights to produce and distribute beer and mead in his hereditary villages, now incorporated into Tarnów. The provisions of the agreement mentioned above came into force on 7 April 1846, after it had been verified by the Court Chancellery in Vienna and approved by the Emperor. Thus the process of separating Grabówka, Strusina, Zabłocie, and Terlikówka from the Tarnów County came to an end. From that moment on, according to the draft of the Statute of the City of Tarnów prepared in 1863 and submitted to the National Sejm in Lviv, the cadastral and political boundaries of the town included the following suburbs outside the town centre: Zawale, Strusina, Zabłocie, Pogwizdów, Grabówka, and Terlikówka.345 In 1870, the enlarged area of Tarnów was divided into four cadastral communes, namely Tarnów, Grabówka, Strusina, and Zabłocie.346 Despite the sale of the lands mentioned above, the Sanguszkos owned the following within the so-called Tarnów County: Tarnowiec, Wólka Tarnowicka, Wałki, and Wierzchosławice. Pogwizdów was an interesting case – an area bordering Zawale to the west, Krzyż to the north, Grabówka to the southeast, and the centre of Tarnów to the west. In 1787, Pogwizdów was a commune with 316 inhabitants living in 50 rural houses.347 In 1846, when Tarnów’s borders were extended, Pogwizdów was incorporated into the town’s administrative boundaries.348 Concurrently, a hospital district had been established in this area, as well as in neighbouring Zawale, featuring a municipal (general) hospital founded in 1833, a Jewish hospital established in 1842, and a military hospital operating in the town.349 The year 1846 marked the end of the first stage of Tarnów’s territorial development in the 19th century. The soundness of the decisions taken by the local authorities at that time is proven by the fact that the area of Tarnów increased sevenfold to 17 km², making it one of the largest towns in Galicia.350 It is no exaggeration to say that between 1845 and 1846, the construction of the ‘Greater Tarnów’ began. In the middle of the 19th century, already after the changes in the town boundaries, the largest area was occupied by Strusina, followed by Grabówka and then the centre of Tarnów with Zawale and Pogwizdów. The most significant changes occurred in Strusina, where the area dedicated to arable land, meadows, gardens, and pastures increased, while other land categories saw a decrease. In the cadastral commune of Tarnów, the area of arable land, gardens, and pastures decreased. In contrast, the area of meadows and the land used for building and road construction projects increased (cf. Tables 3–4). The town authorities spent the second half of the 19th century developing the acquired urban space with new buildings, including public ones. For example, in 1862, responding to public demand, a new school building was erected in the suburb of Strusina.358 A decade later, construction began on the Men’s Faculty School, and the building was opened in 1874. In 1876, the foundation stone was laid for a gymnasium on what was then known as ul. Seminaryjna.359 A little earlier, in 1861, the construction of a building for the Tarnów General Hospi- tal began in the suburb of Pogwizdów. The foundation stone was laid on 15 June of that year. The cost of this significant investment for the town was estimated at 22.5 thousand Rhenish guilders.360 In the years that followed, the General Hospital underwent further modernisation, and in 1909, a new surgical pavilion was constructed. The hospital was connected to the water and sewage system before the First World War.361 Attention was also paid to the development of recreational areas. In 1866, a municipal park, later known as the Park Strzelecki, was established in the Zawale area.362 Investments in the infrastructure of ‘old Tarnow’ were not forgotten either. The works on the pavements in Rynek, ul. Katedralna, Plac Katedralny, as well as in ul. Krakowska and ul. Lwowska intensified. According to Antoni Schneider’s notes, in the 1860s, the town of Tarnów (excluding the suburbs mentioned above) consisted of Rynek, several smaller squares and 16 streets, almost all of which were of sufficient length and width. These streets were, for the most part, ‘gravelled or cobbled.’ 363 356 The cadastral municipality of Tarnow includes Pogwizdów and

The aim was to effectively protect the town from the consequences of the otherwise frequent fires. In the 18th and 19th centuries, fire ravaged Tarnów several times. The most significant fires were in 1735, 1755, 1772, 1792, 1809, and 1814. In 1792, a fire destroyed part of the market square development, which was later rebuilt. As a result, the destroyed arcades were removed. Instead, some of the burghers’ houses were given Baroque-Classical facades, sometimes crowned with balustrade attics.364 In 1809 and 1814, fires destroyed the Bernardine monastery and other buildings.365 In the following years, the nobility court was built on its foundations. The fire of 1809, caused by balloon tests366 carried out by Russians stationed in the town as part of the Russian auxiliary corps officially supporting the French in the war against Austria,367 is particularly remembered by contemporaries. In addition to the Bernardine Monastery, the fire of June 1814 destroyed a part of ul. Żydowska and the synagogue there. The fire also spread to Zabłocie, where many houses burned down. After the fire, Plac Chlebowy, known as Rybny since 1877,368 was built on the cleared land. Also, after 1814, in the area of Plac Pod Dębem (today’s Plac Bohaterów Getta), a place was created where farmers’ horse carts could stop on market days.369 A large fire broke out in 1865. At that time, the fire protection system was found to be inadequate, as the commune had no wells that could be used in the event of a fire.370 The main source of fire-fighting water at that time was the watercourse called Młynówka.371 It was regulated, and its bed was widened in the 19th century.372 The constantly increasing income of the Tarnów commune, which in 1868 amounted to almost 99,000 Rhenish guilders, made it possible to invest in the modernisation of the town’s infrastructure.373 Thus, on the threshold of Galician autonomy, new municipal wells appeared in the urban space of Tarnów, such as the one in Plac Pod Dębem. In the buildings used by the town, wooden stairs were replaced by brick ones. A fire brigade, both professional and voluntary, was established, taking advantage of liberalisation by the Austrian occupiers of the regulations concerning the establishment and operation of so-called non-political associations. Attention was also paid to improving the town’s aesthetics by creating plantations and planting trees along busy streets. In 1865, ul. Seminaryjna was

The development of the railways and the inclusion of Tarnów in the railway network of Galicia and, more widely, of Austria and, later, of the Austro-Hungarian Empire gave a significant boost to the economic, demographic, and spatial development of the town. In time, Tarnów was connected to Leluchów (1876) and, thus, to the Hungarian part of the dual monarchy, and in 1905, it was connected to Russia via a standard-gauge railway line to Szczucin.376 The development of the beaten-track system was not forgotten, however. The aim was to connect smaller towns with Tarnów, which was considered one of the ‘major towns of Galicia.’ Between 1893 and 1909, for example, the 35-kilometre road Tarnów – Żabno – Uście Jezuickie was completely rebuilt and extended in several stages.377 National road no. 57a, which runs from Tarnów eastwards towards Pilzno, was also modernised during this period.378 This modernisation was part of a larger investment (started in 1890) aimed at the reconstruction of road no. 65 between Dębica and Jasło (via Pilzno, Kołaczyce, and Brzostek).379 The proof of the validity of this thesis is the fact that in 1917 the Railway Rolling Stock Repair Plant was established, on the basis of which, in the middle of the last century, the Tarnów Engineering Plant, later transformed into the ‘Ponar-Tarnów’ Engineering Plant, was founded. This enterprise, together with the State Works of Nitrogen Compounds, in the following decades of the 20th century, was the leading production plant in the town, used not only for civil but also for military production.

The First World War was a time of extreme turmoil for the people of Tarnów. The Russian offensive carried out in the late summer and autumn of 1914 resulted in the partial success of the Tsarist army. The Russians occupied most of Galicia. Tarnów was occupied from 10 November 1914 to 5 May 1915. Public buildings were used for military purposes. For example, the Third Gymnasium was turned into a military food store. The use of public buildings by soldiers caused damage to them. However, it was the warfare in the Tarnów area that inflicted the greatest damage on the building fabric and urban infrastructure. During the ‘reconquest of Galicia’ by the armies of the Central Powers between January and April 1915, the town of Tarnów came under bombardment. Artillery shells hit, among others, the Juliusz Słowacki Primary School and the Real School. The Russians were no longer in the town, having left it the day before. It was surrendered without a fight. However, as Franciszek Stefczyk noted: ‘The city itself was a terrible sight. Many houses lay in ruins, streets were strewn with debris, windows shattered, and fences torn down or overturned. The municipal authorities and the civilian inhabitants of the town initially received compensation of ... 15,000 crowns from the Austrian authorities.386 It was not until 1916 that a Building Department of the Central Office for the Reconstruction of Galicia was established in the town.387 It was headed by Franciszek Vetulani, an eminent engineer, expert builder, and social activist.388 Its task was to repair the damage caused by the war to the housing infrastructure. In the first few months of its operation, the Galician Governorate allocated 3 million 300 thousand crowns for reconstruction (mainly for rural households). The poviat of Tarnów received 400,000 crowns from this amount.389 How much of this sum went to the town? We do not know. What we do know is that by 1917, the poviat of Tarnów had managed to rebuild most of its destroyed schools with funds from the Central Office. Unfortunately, in other instances, residents of Tarnów largely financed the reconstruction costs through funds raised by social organisations like the Ducal-Episcopal Relief Committee for War Victims.390

Tarnów officially came under Polish rule. The first weeks and months of independence were extremely difficult for the inhabitants of Tarnów. The town’s residents had to contend with widespread common crime and problems of supply. The latter mainly concerned hard coal as a source of fuel.396 To make matters worse, the town became the scene of mass bandit attacks on the civilian population.397 In these circumstances, attempts were made to restore the town to its pre-war urbanisation level. The initial actions of the municipal authorities were directed towards averting the demographic deurbanisation of the town. Various factors contributed to this state of affairs, ranging from losses due to direct hostilities in 1914–1918 and later 1918–1920 to deaths caused by epidemic diseases, such as the Spanish flu, through to emigration. In August of the following year, a similar amount was borrowed from the Credit Union of Towns of Małopolska to regulate the flow of the Wątok stream partially. Unfortunately, all post-war investment activities were exclusively of a shortterm nature. The ongoing economic depression and the consequent inefficiency of public finances, including those of the municipality, led to a dearth of significant building investments. During the first half of the 1920s, the authorities in Tarnów were preoccupied with securing funds for the town’s day-to-day operation. In March 1923, the Town Council was compelled to secure short-term loans from banks to maintain liquidity and meet administrative expenses.402 Among the most significant construction projects completed in Tarnów before 1925 was the inauguration of the Marzenie Cinema Theatre (then referred to as the Light Theatre), which belonged to the Tarnów branch of the People’s School Society (Towarzystwo Szkoły Ludowej, TSL). The hall, considered modern for its time, served as a theatre, cinema, and lecture hall with a seating capacity of 700. Constructed between 1922 and 1924, the investment was funded by a loan from the General Savings Bank (Powszechna Kasa Oszczędności, PKO).403

The TSL building was not the only public utility building that enriched the urban landscape in the 1920s. In 1926, a new building for the Railwaymen’s Union Circle House was erected, housing not only commercial spaces but also hosting one of the banks, the Union’s library, the Railwaymen’s Choir headquarters, and an assembly hall. 1927 proved to be a significant year in Tarnów’s investment agenda. In March, with the help of a loan from the Ministry of Public Works, the town council decided to construct a shelter for the increasing number of individuals affected by homelessness. Nearly simultaneously, efforts were made to secure a loan for the municipality. This loan was intended for expanding the municipal slaughterhouse, erecting a girls’ school in the Strusina district, establishing a pavilion for the infectious diseases ward at Tarnów Hospital, and modernising the market halls and the market area in general.404 The majority of these initiatives were executed in the ensuing months and years. For instance, the infectious diseases ward, designed to accommodate one hundred patients, was completed in 1935.405 Despite economic challenges, the transition from the 1920s to the 1930s in Tarnów was characterised by the construction of new schools. The Klementyna Hoffmanowa Women’s School was particularly pressing for a new building due to overcrowding and fungal infestation in the old premises. The decision to commence its construction was made in 1927. However, owing to various objective factors, including the economic downturn, this significant educational project was only finalised in January 1935.406 In September 1931, the new building of the Eliza Orzeszkowa Private Gymnasium for Girls was inaugurated in ul. Tertila.407 In 1937, the above-mentioned TSL opened a Private Mechanical School for Men in Tarnów, for which a new building was constructed at the junction of ul. Staszica and ul. Batorego.408 The modernisation of the urban space in Tarnów in the interwar period also included the so-called green areas. It is worth mentioning that during that time that Planty Kolejowe (Railway Green) was created, later renamed Planty im. Józefa Jakubowskiego (Józef Jakubowski’s Green) in memory of the interwar deputy mayor of Tarnów, who initiated the creation of the park. Modernisation also extended to Park Strzelecki, which was enclosed by a fence.409 Simultaneously, efforts were made to organise the cemetery space. Consequently, a Cemetery Commission was established in Tarnów, engaging in activities aimed at the expansion and renovation of the cemeteries in Tarnów and its environs. One of its notable achievements was the establishment of the New Cemetery in the village of Krzyż near Tarnów in 1928.410 Shortly after that, cemeteries were established in Klikowa (1931) and Rzędzin (1933).411

One of the challenges faced by Tarnów in the 1920s was the confusion surrounding street names and their signage. Hence, among the tasks entrusted to the municipal authorities was the assignment of names to previously unnamed streets, which had been extensively laid out in the early decades of the 20th century. Following public consultations, numerous streets in Tarnów were given names. Their selection was not arbitrary but rather based on the area’s topography, historical significance, and current use. Consequently, the residents of Tarnów became richer with the following streets, among others: Droga do Huty, Fabryczna, Do Prochowni, Garbarska, and Spadzista. Many streets were named after historical figures associated with Polish history and culture, such as Aleksander Fredro or Joachim Lelewel.412 In April 1929, aiming to streamline communication and facilitate navigation in the progressively expanding city, the city council adopted a resolution mandating the installation of uniform enamel informational plaques displaying street names and house numbers throughout Tarnów.413 The process of beautifying public spaces in Tarnów continued into the 1930s despite the objective difficulties related to the economic situation. As early as 1930, the millstream in the area of ul. Ogrodowa was filled in.414 In the subsequent years, several buildings owned by the city, including those on ul. Wałowa and ul.
