and restoration.415 Unfortunately, both the Magistrate and the poviat authorities were unable to execute all the necessary investments, which prompted justified resentment among the city’s residents. On 21 March 1930, the editor of the Tarnów periodical, Hasło, raised the issue of the urgent need to renovate ul. Lwowska, posing the rhetorical question: Does it still belong to Tarnów? As he pointed out: ‘A few days ago, I had to pass through ul. Ochronek next to ul. Lwowska. Suddenly, I found myself in the middle of ul. Lwowska, unable to escape the muddy swamp. I pondered whether this district still belonged to the town or whether I already was in some forsaken village.’416 A similar sentiment was echoed by a journalist from the weekly Wiadomości Tarnowskie in October 1934. In the pages of the magazine, he wrote: ‘If the Poviat Roads Office were to follow the example of the Town Council and finally consider the reconstruction of ul. Lwowska, which is such an eyesore in Tarnów, it would bring true relief to the inhabitants of the eastern part of the town.’ 417 Other transportation routes also left much to be desired, as evidenced by the fact that in 1937, only 12% of the public roads in Tarnów were paved.418 Some streets required extensive repairs and street lighting. Residents themselves submitted petitions to the town council, hoping for their demands to be addressed. One such petition concerned the repair of ul. Krakowska leading towards the railway works.419 The devastation of streets and public squares was a result of the aforementioned financial catastrophe. To exacerbate the situation, in July 1934, the city and its vicinity experienced the most significant flood since 1887. A three-meter high flood wave inundated the area beyond the railway line toward Zgłobice. Water from the Wątok stream flooded the suburb of Huta, where wooden quarters for the urban dispossessed were located.420 The water supply system of Tarnów suffered damage, as did the lower-level facilities of the State Works of Nitrogen Compounds in Mościce.421 After the high water subsided, many residents from the poorer districts of Tarnów and neighbouring villages were left homeless. Before winter set in, bunkhouses for people affected by homelessness constructed in Pogwizdów were utilised to accommodate some of the flood victims.422 Plans for the reconstruction of ul. Lwowska, notoriously poorly paved with cobblestones at the time, were drafted in the autumn of 1938.423 This investment was likely associated with the construction of the Church

of the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus, which had been underway on this street since 1935.424 In the context of the aforementioned accomplishments, the figure of Witold Giżbert Studnicki deserves mention. Born in Kormanice near Przemyśl, this architect, conservationist, and painter became closely associated with Tarnów during the interwar period. After completing his architectural studies at the Lviv Polytechnic and serving as an assistant at the university for several years, he was appointed as the director of the Tarnów Municipal Building Department in 1927. He held this position until 1943. Studnicki was responsible for several significant building projects carried out in Tarnów during the interwar period. These included the construction of the municipal slaughterhouse in 1929, the new bus station, the market hall, and the residential estates in ul. Dwernickiego in Pogwizdów.425 Additionally, he made substantial contributions to the preservation of historical monuments. Among his most notable projects in Tarnów were the conservation of the Town Hall and the remnants of the town walls, the restoration of the 18th-century Bernardine Church, the renovation of Renaissance burgher houses around Rynek, and the reconstruction in 1936 of one of Tarnów’s historically significant streets, ul. Wielkie Schody.426 During the renovation of ul. Wielkie Schody, a stone mascaron, now an emblematic feature of the street, was crafted by the esteemed sculptor Henryk Hochman.427 In the case of the old mediaeval church of the Bernardine Fathers, Witold Giżbert Studnicki undertook its partial regothicisation by revealing old Gothic frescoes on the walls of the former chancel. Showing his commitment to the preservation of Tarnów’s heritage and history, he co-founded the Social Committee for Monument Restoration and later the Society for Monument Conservation in Tarnów.428 In 1934, thanks to the efforts of the residents of Tarnów and Witold Giżbert Studnicki himself, the Kraków District Conservation Officer declared this area a historic zone to extend legal protection to the town centre’s historic space. The legally protected area included the buildings and the area bounded by ul. Wałowa, ul. Szeroka, and ul. Bernardyńska, from Plac Morawskiego to Plac św. Ducha, including Plac św. Ducha and ul. Targowa (up to ul. Wałowa).429

Studium his- Besides public construction, the years 1919–1939 marked a period of residential development in Tarnów. According to data from the 1921 Census, the total number of buildings within the town’s administrative boundaries was 2,205, of which 2,180 were exclusively designated for housing. This amounted to an average of sixteen persons per dwelling. The majority (68.4%) of houses had one or two flats. Predominantly, especially in less urbanised areas, single-story dwellings prevailed, accounting for 68.6% of all dwellings (see Table 6). Most residences consisted of one or two rooms, while three-story buildings were rare (see Table 7). This urban development pattern resulted from the incorporation within the town limits of rural areas, the vast majority of which lacked modern multi-storey buildings. In these areas, villa construction remained highly popular.

As far as housing was concerned, the resolution passed by the Town Council on 18 May 1927, mandating the commencement of a housing estate development on the Infułackie lands, proved to be significant. A bit earlier, the construction of tenement houses in the Pogwizdów area had been initiated. In this latter case, the investment persisted until the outbreak of the Second World War.430 Furthermore, by the end of 1927, approximately a hundred licenses had been issued for the construction of private houses, primarily single-storey ones. While this figure remained modest compared to the pre-First World War years, it marked a notable improvement from the stagnation experienced since 1918. The State works of Nitrogen Compounds and their significance for the spatial development of Tarnów In the initial years following Poland’s regaining of independence, the development of key industries crucial for the Polish economy was initiated. Among these was the chemical industry. A significant figure in its development was Ignacy Mościcki, associated with the Lviv Polytechnic, who served as the director of the chemical factory in Chorzów before becoming the President of the Republic of Poland. In the mid-1920s, the Chemical Research Institute was established in Warsaw. Its leadership decided to select the area surrounding the then Małopolska town of Tarnów as the site for a factory specialising in the production of nitrogen compounds, essential for various applications, including agriculture.431 On 12 March 1927, a contract was signed with the Sanguszko family for the sum of US$ 207,000 to facilitate the realisation of these plans. This amount was utilised to purchase a 670-hectare estate intended to serve as the foundation for a new hub for the chemical industry in Poland.432 The choice of location for the new investment was no accident. The villages of Świerczków and Dąbrówka Infułacka, adjacent to Tarnów, boasted favourable geographical positioning and excellent transportation links. The proximity to rivers, including the navigable Wisła, as well as major railway lines passing through the area, ensured a secure supply of raw materials crucial for the plant’s operations. Furthermore, the relatively short distance between Tarnów and the former Sanguszko estates and important industrial regions such as the Dąbrowa Basin in Upper Silesia, the so-called Kraków Basin, and the oil-rich areas concentrated in the then Lviv Voivodeship, played a significant role.433 Additionally, the proximity of a big poviat town, which Tarnów was considered to be in the 1920s, also favoured the choice of location. According to Warsaw, the region’s demographic and social potential, marked by numerous schools and a substantial presence of small industries and crafts, which could potentially support the nitrogen plant workforce, was seen as pivotal for the plant’s success. Another contributing factor in choosing Świerczków and Dąbrówka Infułacka was the well-developed municipal infrastructure in Tarnów, which could be utilised for the plant’s establishment, including the operational municipal power station and water supply system.434

The decision of the local town council tipped the scales in favour of Tarnów. In a resolution adopted on 14 February 1927, it committed ‘to address, at its own expense, responsibility, and risk, any difficulties that might arise in the areas of Świerczków and Dąbrówka Infułacka in connection with the construction and subsequent operation of the factory due to existing plants and water pipes in these areas, or other interests of the Municipality of Tarnów.’435 Less than three months later, on 5 May 1927, the first workers appeared on the construction site in Świerczków. The following months saw the construction of an emergency housing estate (18 June) and a railway siding (2 August).436 The main phase of construction began in 1928, with the construction of the mechanical workshop (16 January), the production halls (28 February), the on-site power station (14 May), and the salt stores (17 Septem- 431 The first concepts of building a nitrogen factory in the Tarnów area appeared in 1923–1924. The last production hall was inaugurated on 15 December.437 In addition to the factory buildings, the creation of a housing estate for the employees of the State Works of Nitrogen Compounds proved to be a significant investment. According to urban planning assumptions, the planned housing estate was designed to have a villa-like character, with each family allocated a small garden. By the end of the 1920s, twelve houses were constructed for the families of officials and four more for the workers. The latter were single-storey and made of brick. Despite the dynamic progress of the project, providing adequate housing for all interested workers within two years proved challenging. Therefore, in 1929, fourteen temporary wooden dwellings were erected to be replaced in the future by detached houses with their own gardens.438

With the commencement of the construction of the State Works of Nitrogen Compounds in the areas of Świerczków and Dąbrówka Infułacka in Tarnów, discussions began to intensify regarding the necessity of incorporating both villages, along with Chyszów, Gumniska, Rzędzin, and Klikowa, into the town. In 1927, negotiations were initiated regarding the terms of integrating these mentioned communes into a single administrative entity. The Tarnów authorities hoped that this would complete the process of incremental urbanisation of Tarnów, which had been underway since the 19th century. On 16 May 1928, the Town Council made two pivotal decisions. The first decision was to reject the conditions proposed by the authorities of the aforementioned rural communes for their incorporation into the town. Subsequently, another decision was made, directing the mayor of Tarnów to petition the state authorities to forcibly incorporate the surrounding villages into the town’s administrative boundaries. Tarnów’s councillors were confident that this decision would be applauded and met with approval in Warsaw. Józef Jakubowski, the town assessor and second deputy mayor of Tarnów, amidst the enthusiasm of the gathered councillors and members of the Magistrate, after the resolution was passed, was said to exclaim, ‘Long live Greater Tarnów!’ However, contrary to the optimistic expectations of Tarnów’s inhabitants, Chyszów, Gumniska, Świerczków, Rzędzin, and Klikowa were not incorporated at that time.439 It would take until the 1950s for the plans from 1928 to materialise for all parties involved. While Józef Jakubowski’s somewhat prematurely announced plan to expand ‘Greater Tarnów’ was postponed for another time, the merger of the communes of Dąbrówka Infułacka and Świerczków into the single commune of Mościce became a reality. The decision was made in July 1929.440 Concurrently, the construction of the Mościce railway station commenced in the area of Dąbrówka Infułacka.441 With the establishment of the Mościce commune, the authorities of Tarnów, fully aware of the role and expansive nature of the newly established nitrogen plant, decided that industrial development in Tarnów would be confined to areas situated between the Kraków – Tarnów and Tarnów – Nowy Sącz railway lines.442 To sum up these considerations, in the interwar period – according to the concept adopted by Zdzisław Simche – Tarnów, within its administrative boundaries of that time, was divided into three main areas. The first consisted of the actual, physiognomically compact town. The second comprised the oldest suburbs, ‘merged with the town,’ or located in its immediate vicinity. The outer limits of this zone were defined by the economic functions of the suburb and the settlement associated with it. According to Simche, the third and final type of built landscape was marked by ‘islands of urban settlement’ situated away from the town centre and amidst areas with typically rural architecture.443 The Old Town, dominated by brick buildings, was regarded as the town’s core. Similarly, the areas located to the south and east of the Old Town were heavily urbanised. At that time, the suburb of Zabłocie was connected to the Old

Grabówka, situated to the east of the town, was considered an autonomous district in the interwar period, with a strong emphasis on trade and economic activity. The suburbs to the south of the Old Town and Rynek were characterised by modernity, largely due to the presence of industrial plants linked to the railway network passing through this part of the town. Here, we refer to three districts: Terlikówka, Zamoście, and Strusina. The first of these was divided into two parts: agricultural and urban. The agricultural areas were directly adjacent to the railway station, while the urban-industrial areas surrounded the local four brickworks, military barracks, and the railway station branch. The district of Zamoście was already considered fully urbanised thanks to the urban development around the railway workshops and the so-called Kolonia Kolejowa. The third of the listed districts, Strusina, was described before the Second World War as a ‘transitional area’ – ‘ephemeral.’444 Its western areas were still characterised by strongly rural architecture. The inhabitants of this area were still engaged in agriculture. The opposite was true of eastern Strusina, where the majority of the population was already engaged in urban activities. In the years between the wars, Strusina underwent a gradual but systematic urbanisation in connection with the town’s industrial development. At the same time, ul. Klikowa was expected to retain its agricultural character for a longer time, as this part of Tarnów was bypassed by the so-called ‘big industry.’ During the Second Polish Republic, the areas between Grabówka and Zabłocie, where new housing was built, took on a modern appearance. An interesting case was the then-independent village of Rzędzin, which, bordering on Grabówka, underwent gradual economic urbanisation.445 The spatial urbanisation of the village had to wait until the post-war years.

On Friday, 1 September 1939, the Third German Reich launched aggression against Poland. From the first hours of the war, anxiety and fear pervaded Tarnów, caused in part by German bombers that appeared over the city. Their target was the State Works of Nitrogen Compounds in Mościce. From 3 September, German bombs began to target the railway station and railway infrastructure. Several houses in the vicinity of the station on ul. Narutowicza were destroyed. The general hospital building was severely damaged. Chaos gripped the city. On 7 September, Tarnów was deserted as inhabitants of neighbouring villages hurriedly left. Those who didn’t evacuate sought refuge in their homes. Around noon, the Germans en- tered Tarnów.446 For the people of Tarnów, a long German occupation which was to end only in January 1945, began. These years were marked by the extermination of civilians, persecution of Polish culture, and the plundering of material goods and economic resources. The Jewish inhabitants of Tarnów and nearby communities were particularly targeted for biological extermination. A tangible expression of the repression against Jews was the destruction of Jewish synagogues and prayer houses on 9 November 1939 and on 19 June 1942, followed by the establishment of the Tarnów Ghetto by the decision of German City Commissioner Gustav Hackbarth.447 The area of this ghetto, the largest in the Kraków district, was to occupy a small part of the former Jewish quarter in the Grabówka area. The Jews of Tarnów and those from neighbouring villages were crowded into the quarter bounded by ul. Jasna (from the east), ul. Lwowska (from the south), ul. Wałowa and ul. E. Goldhammera (from the west), and ul. Adama Mickiewicza and ul. Polna (from the north). The streets and squares around which the Jewish population was concentrated and, from 22 June 1942, confined to were ul. Folwarczna, ul. Kupiecka, Plac Pod Dębem, Plac Dożywocie, Plac Magdeburski, ul. Polna, ul. Gołębia, ul. Wschodnia, partly ul. Szpitalna and ul. Nowodąbrowska, ul. Starodąbrowska, ul. Widok, ul. Krupnicza, ul. Ochronek, ul. Spadzista, ul. Krawiecka, ul. Stolarska, ul. Jasna, and ul. Lwowska with even-numbered houses.448 The ghetto was liquidated in stages. The major liquidation action took place between 2 and 4 September 1943. The Jews of Tarnów were deported to Auschwitz, the labour camp in Szebnie near Jasło, and the camp in Płaszów. The last transport to Płaszów took place in February 1944.449 About 20,000 people from the Tarnów ghetto were deported and murdered. Only a few survived the extermination. The civilian holocaust of the Second World War left its mark on the post-war demographic potential of the town, whose population fell to 33,000450. The hecatomb that the Second World War, taking into account the data from the 1931 census, resulted in a decrease in the population of Tarnów by 12,127 people. It was only in the 1950s, thanks to the incorporation of Mościce and other surrounding villages, that the population of Tarnów returned to its pre-war level.451

Jelonek, Ludność miast (as n. 381), p. 52. uRBaNISaTION IN ThE PERIOd Of ThE PEOPlE’S REPuBlIC Of POlaNd aNd ThE yEaRS Of ThE ThIRd REPuBlIC On the night of 17–18 January 1945, the last units of the German 17th Field Army, commanded by General Friedrich von Schutz, left Tarnów, fearing encirclement by the Red Army. In order to impede their pursuit, the Germans destroyed the road and railway bridges over the Wątok stream, causing damage to the churches in the Burek and Terlikówka districts.452 In Tarnów, the railway station, the goods station and the telephone exchange located in the post office building were destroyed. It is estimated that nearly 50% of the buildings in Tarnów were damaged to varying degrees after the Germans departed. On the morning of 18 January, the first units of the 60th Army of the 1st Belorussian Front entered the town. On the same day, an eight-man delegation of the Provisional Government of the Republic of Poland arrived from Rzeszów to take over the authorities in Tarnów and establish a new order on behalf of the communist government. Stanislaw Kroch, the organiser and first head of the Tarnów Public Security Office, who had been trained in Kuybyshev by the Soviet People’s Commissariat for Internal Affairs, the notorious NKVD, was appointed as the head of the group.453 Another member of the Rzeszów ‘Initiative Group’, Jozef Lib, headed the Poviat Starosty.454 Ludwik Mysiak (also known as Mysak) was entrusted with the authority over the city. His tasks included the creation of structures for the Citizens’ Militia, as well as the reactivation of local education and social services.455 The citizens of Tarnów entered a new chapter in their history, which lasted for almost 44 years.

In 1945, Tarnów covered an area of 1,761 hectares. The crimes committed by the German occupiers against the inhabitants of the town and the region caused the town’s population to fall to 30,000.456 The people of Tarnów had to adjust to a new post-war reality. A reality that reshaped the political 452 K. Moskal, Kronika Tarnowa, Tarnów 2015, p. 200. 453 Ibidem. 454 W. Paryła, Przemiany polityczne i społeczne w latach 1945–1975, [in:] 455 I. Faltyn-Pokrywka, Mysak (Mysiak) Ludwik, [in:] Encyklopedia 456 J. Szczerbak, Plany zagospodarowania przestrzennego (as n. 450), p. 315; Tarnów. Wielki przewodnik, vol. 15 (as n. 450), p. 207. scene at both national and local levels. One of the first decisions of the new local authorities was to organise the territory of Tarnów by drafting a general plan for the town. This task was entrusted to a 1929 graduate of the Warsaw University of Technology, an outstanding architect and town planner, already successful in pre-war Poland: Władysław Antoni Wieczorkiewicz.457 Between 1945 and 1946, he designed a plan for Tarnów based on the concentric development of buildings around the Old Town. Wieczorkiewicz attached great importance to the development of the transport system, with the construction of new roads parallel to the existing railway line. A new arterial road was also planned between the river Biała and the western outskirts of the city, linking Tarnów’s northern and southern districts. Along the eastern border of Tarnów, a connection between ul. Nowodąbrowska and Tuchowska was to be built. In addition, the spaces between the suburbs and the town centre should be connected by parks and gardens, which corresponded to the ideas of the ‘garden city’ already known in the 19th century thanks to the British town planner Ebenezer Howard. Wieczorkiewicz envisioned the town as a supra-regional industrial centre, a natural consequence of its location within the pre-war Central Industrial District. For this reason, he planned 457 Władysław Antoni Wieczorkiewicz (b. 23 December 1896 – d. 12 March 1948) – architect, town-planner, member of the Association of Polish Architects. He was a graduate of the Faculty of Architecture at the Warsaw University of Technology. In the 1930s, he was head of the Office for Urban Measurements and Development at the Voivodeship Office in Warsaw. At that time, he became famous for drawing up plans for the reconstruction of Wyszków, Grodzisk Mazowiecki, Płock, Zamość, and Włocławek. He took part as a co-designer in competitions for, among others, the project for the regulation and development of Poznań (1931). In 1937, he was awarded first prize in a competition for planning the city of Rivne in Volhynia. After the war, he was appointed head of the Urban Planning Division of the Regional Spatial Planning Directorate in Kraków. It was then that he started working at the Department of Urban Planning of the Krakow University of Technology. His post-1945 projects include, apart from the plan to rebuild Tarnów, the urban plan of Limanowa, Chrzanów, and Trzebinia. Wieczorkiewicz died in 1948. He was buried in the Rakowicki Cemetery in Kraków. https://www.archimemory.pl/pokaz/ wladyslaw_antoni_wieczorkiewicz,17145 (access: 30 October 2023); W. Przegon, Draft of the Zamość development Plan of 1939, Geomatics, Landmanagement and Landscape, No. 1, 2023, pp. 75–86 (DOI: http:// dx.doi.org/10.15576/GLL/2023.1.75).

for Tarnów to have a population of up to 50,000.458 Consequently, he did not plan for any areas for the development of multi-family housing, limiting himself to indicating areas for the development of single-family, single-storey buildings, which had hitherto dominated the urban landscape (see Table 8).459 As it is widely acknowledged, these estimates proved to be inaccurate, as in the following decades, Tarnów became one of the most demographically developed cities in Małopolska. The history of post-war spatial urbanisation in Tarnów is inextricably linked with that of the neighbouring communes. Suffice it to say that Władysław Wieczorkiewicz’s town planning project included not only the existing administrative boundaries of the town but also the village of Świerczków – known before the war as Mościce, which was then an independent administrative unit. The plan to incorporate Mościce into Tarnów emerged immediately after the war. This step was seen as a natural progression for the city’s development. As per docu- 458 AWUOZ, inventory no. 2774 I: Tarnów. Studium historyczno- 459 J. Szczerbak, Plany zagospodarowania przestrzennego (as n. 450), pp. 460 J. Szczerbak, Plany zagospodarowania przestrzennego (as n. 450), ments preserved by the Krakow Voivodeship Office, the first administrative changes concerning Mościce were initiated in the autumn of 1946. At that time, the Presidium of the Mościce Commune National Council asked the management of the local State Works of Nitrogen Compounds for an opinion on the integration of several neighbouring communes into the unitary commune of Mościce and the creation of a larger collective commune. On 23 November 1946, the plant authorities issued an opinion on the matter. They sent it to the Ministry of Public Administration through the Association of the Fertiliser Industry.461 The signatories of the document, Bronisław Twardzicki, Stanisław Żuczkiewicz, Czesław Łachecki and Kazimierz Zawistowski, considered it necessary at that time to incorporate only the hamlets of Kępa Bogumiłowicka and the commune of Zbylitowska Góra into Mościce, without other typically rural settlements. The rationale provided to support the expansion of the Mościce commune, albeit in a limited scope, is as follows:

‘The commune of Mościce is a typical factory settlement where the element of workers is overwhelming. The industrial plants located on the territory of the commune, such as the Factory [State Works of Nitrogen Compounds – K.M.], the Regional Power Station, the Gasworks, and the Tarnów Waterworks, due to their constant growth and development, attract more and more workers, whose living conditions, aspirations, and cultural and social needs are different from those of the peasant population of the neighbouring rural settlements. Every factory worker aspires to own a house with a garden, in keeping with their cultural requirements as workers in large industry. The entire communal economy has been adapted to these cultural requirements and has consistently endeavoured to meet these needs and to develop Mościce into a model factory settlement with urban characteristics [...]. Since the creative factor in the economic life of Mościce is and will be the factory worker, it is only right that he should have the exclusive right to decide on the economic plan and its implementation in the area where he lives and works. The creation of a collective commune, in which Mościce would be the seat of the commune but would itself be a commune, means the complete overturning of the present economic direction of Mościce and the transfer of the distribution of Mościce’s income from the competence of the present Mościce Commune Council [...] to the competence of external factors.’ 462 From the preceding information, it is evident that according to individuals associated with the Nitrogen Factory, finances were the main factor blocking the enlargement of the Mościce commune. The management of the State Works of Nitrogen Compounds was strongly determined to maintain the existing administrative boundaries. Their influence was significant enough to prompt intervention from the Ministry of Public Administration.463 The residents of the villages concerned held a different view, expressing their desire to merge with the Mościce commune through local referendums. After many weeks of extensive consultations and correspondence, the Poviat National Council in Tarnów decided on 28 August 461 ANK (as n. 12), Kraków Voivodeship Office, ref. no. The first three were separated from the commune of Gumniska and the last from the commune of Wojnicz, which at that time belonged to the Brzesko poviat.464 Ultimately, the borders of Tarnów were altered on 15 December 1948 by the decree of Władysław Wolski, Minister of Public Administration, published in the Journal of Laws in January 1949.465 On 31 January 1949, the ‘transfer activities connected with the transfer of the above­ mentioned villages’ to the Mościce commune were carried out.466 The development of Mościce in the post-war period led to attempts to adopt local spatial development plans. In 1948, such plans were prepared for the needs of the Kraków-based ‘Miastoprojekt’ company by Wanda Pencakowska from Lviv, who was then a lecturer at the Faculty of Architecture at the Kraków University of Technology.467 Pencakowska’s vision, like Wieczorkiewicz’s, was not realised. However, the next development plans for the area were not long in coming. Before this happened, the year 1951 marked a pivotal moment for Mościce and Tarnów. It was then that the decision was taken to incorporate several neighbouring communes, including Mościce, Chyszów, Klikowa, Gumniska, Rzędziny, and a part of Koszyce Wielkie into Tarnów. As a result, Tarnów expanded to encompass 5,490 hectares.468 The incorporation of the communes mentioned above into the city was the completion of a process that began in 1845–1846 – a process that should be described as the construction of the ‘Greater Tarnów.’ Between 1951 and 1954, town planners from the aforementioned Kraków’s ‘Miastoprojekt’ company undertook the task of drawing up plans for the urban development of Tarnów. The idea of the town planners was to plan a city with a target population of 100,000, including 9,500 in Świerczków – Mościce.469 In this case, the planners adopted a concept based on the topography of the town, the central point of which was a ‘hill descending in terraces in all directions.’470 The centre of gravity of the housing development was shifted to the area to the east of the Old

Starodąbrowska)471, the construction of a second centre for new housing in the ‘old Tarnów’ was planned. However, despite the ambitious plans, the reality was less optimistic. On the one hand, there was the prospect of new housing estates. Still, on the other, the areas recently incorporated into Tarnów were lagging in terms of civilisation. Suffice it to say that in 1954, the inhabitants of the Rzędzina district (annexed in 1951) complained about the lack of lighting and communication with other parts of Tarnów, as well as the deplorable state of the roads.472 In other parts of the city, some buildings, even those built between the wars, were said to be in need of repair. It was the case, for example, in Świerczków, where in 1955, 49 houses were classified as in urgent need of repair.473 The expansion of Tarnów’s city limits, successfully completed in 1951, allowed the municipal authorities to invest in new areas of the city. Undoubtedly, the main beneficiary of such a solution was Mościce, where construction of housing started as early as 1949. The first blocks of flats, built on the workers’ estate, were completed. The first tenants of the new flats were the former inhabitants of the temporary wooden dwellings built in al. Lipowa.474 By 1955, 33 blocks of flats with 820 flats had been completed in Tarnów as part of the Six-Year Plan. In the following five years, from 1956 to 1960, another 60 blocks with 1,478 flats were built. This investment was financed by the National Council, local workplaces and, to a lesser extent, housing cooperatives.475 Apart from Tarnów, of course, most of the new housing was built in the district of Świerczków, on land previously earmarked for the construction of an ‘emergency housing estate’, which, according to the 1954 plan, was intended to accommodate 9,500 individuals employed at the Feliks Dzierżyński Nitrogen Works in Tarnów.476 It is worth noting that the expansion of the plant in Świerczków-Mościce led to a substantial increase in employment, which had a snowball effect and caused a significant housing shortage. In order to solve this problem, in the second half of the 1950s, the Voivodeship Urban Planning Office in Krakow developed the concept of expanding the city to the northwest. The planners’ premise was to create a new city centre close to the city’s industrial area.477 To this end, the administrative area of Tarnów was enlarged again in 1958. The village of Krzyż was incorporated into the city.478 As a result of this decision, by the early 1960s, Tarnów covered an area of 6,851 hectares.479 How-

In the near future (up to 1980), the expansion of the city’s boundaries would lay the foundations for the creation of the Tarnów Industrial District venture, which would bring together not only large industrial enterprises but also service providers and educational and cultural institutions.480 The preparation of successive zoning plans and the resulting incremental urbanisation of the city provided the impetus for launching large-scale housing construction. In the 1970s, new housing estates were built on sites adjacent to the factory grounds (in ul. Marchlewskiego, now 11 Listopada), and the old ones, dating from the inter-war period, were extended.481 The Za Torem housing estate was given a new face, and with the support of the Nitrogen Works, more empty lots were filled with detached houses. The city’s development plans also included the creation of the Koszyce I housing estate. In response to the significant housing demand, the Kapro estate was established as a temporary measure, with brick and even wooden structures. Over time, the housing infrastructure improved dramatically. In 1970, modern blocks of flats were put into use in the Strusina housing estate, where the workers of the nitrogen plant were to be housed.482 Suffice it to say that in the five years from 1961 to 1965, 74 blocks of flats were completed in Tarnów, housing 2,811 families.483 A pivotal moment in the urbanisation of Tarnów occurred with the decision of the Economic Committee of the Council of Ministers of 14 June 1966484. At that time, the main directions for the development of Tarnów, as well as for its environmental protection in connection with the pollution caused by the Nitrogen Works, were outlined. Following the government’s decisions, 9,200 flats were built, the water, sewerage, and gas networks were extended, the construction of a modern sewage treatment plant began, and the construction of a new bus station was commissioned.

The construction of the ‘Świt’ department store aimed to enhance the retail and service offerings. In 1969–1974, as part of the measures taken by the Council of Ministers, the area northeast of the Old Town, extending towards Rzędzin, was developed, where two housing estates were designed and built: The 25-lecia PRL [25th Anniversary of the Polish People’s Republic] (now, after decommunisation, called Osiedle Niepodległości [Independence Estate]) and Słoneczne. With the establishment of the so-called first and second protection zones in 1971, which separated the Nitrogen Works from residential areas (not counting the already established ‘emergency housing estate’), an absolute ban on the construction of residential buildings in the vicinity of the factory was introduced. In this way, a part of Chyszów was designated as a ‘green area’ instead of being used for building after it had first been redesignated in the city’s urban plan. In Kolonia Kolejowa, on the other hand, worker allotment gardens were established. In addition, the green belt area in the Świerczków neighbourhood was increased.490 The growing population and housing development in Tarnów posed new challenges for the central and local authorities and the management of the Tarnów Nitrogen Works in providing adequate educational and cultural facilities for the inhabitants of Tarnów. Daycare centres, kindergartens, and schools were built. In 1955, for example, the construction of a metalworking school with dormitories and workshops, daycare centres at the Mechanical Works and in the Grabówka area, a primary school in Mościce, a technical school at the Nitrogen Works, etc. commenced.491 At the same time, Tarnów launched a thorough redevelopment of the city, focusing on the old town and its surrounding areas. The systematic development of Tarnów necessitated the expansion of its administrative boundaries. Therefore, in 1979, the Voivodeship National Council in Tarnów adopted an ambitious plan prepared by a team led by the architect and town planner Janina Szałapkowa. It proposed incorporating additional areas into Tarnów, including the following villages: Wola Rzędzińska, Koszyce Wielkie, Zbylitowska Góra (in its entirety), and Biała. According to the plan, Tarnów would have a population of 130,000 and an area of 10,900 hectares.493 However, these plans were not realised, and today, the mentioned villages are independent rural administrative units forming part of the rural commune of Tarnów.494 The failure of Janina Szałapkowa’s plan is likely linked to the political and economic changes of the late 1980s and early 1990s, but also the changes in the demographic and socio-occupational structure of Tarnów at the end of the last century and the beginning of the present. Nevertheless, as early as 1995, the futuristic plans of the town planners allowed for the development of Tarnów as a centre with a population of 220,000.495

As indicated in the provided data, the population of Tarnów was just under 113,000 on 31 December 2008. In reality, the number was slightly higher, fluctuating around 116,000, as 2,887 people had the right of temporary residence in Tarnów. Unfortunately, these figures were far from satisfactory, as the city’s population decreased by 931 people compared to 2007. The immediate and main reason for this was rising unemployment in the city and region. At that time, almost 10,000 people of working age were registered with the Poviat Job Centre.500 In 2010, the demographic outlook in Tarnów was even less optimistic. According to the statistics, the city had 112,267 registered residents and 2,832 temporary residents, thus totalling 115,099. This reflects a nearly 1% decline in Tarnów’s population over two years (since December 2008). In raw numbers, 1,138 people left Tarnów during this brief period.501 The city’s depopulation has accelerated in recent years. In 2017, the total population of Tarnów was 109,650. The following year, it was already 109,062, while in 2019, the number of inhabitants of Tarnów was only 108,470. Two factors influenced the observed demographic 500 K. Moskal, Kronika Tarnowa (as n. 452), p. 291 501 Ibidem, pp. 291, 298. decline. The first was related to internal and external emigration (the migration balance was negative and calculated at 646 people), and the second, equally worrying, resulted from negative natural growth. I want to mention that in 2019 alone, while 1,142 people died, only 897 children were born in Tarnow.502 Despite the apparent depopulation of Tarnów, its spatial and architectural urbanisation continued. The municipal and poviat authorities made further investments crucial for the residents. These include the completion by Tarnów Waterworks of a modern water treatment plant in Zbylitowska Góra (2008) and the modernisation of the building of the former Mościce Cultural Centre (2010). Recreational and sports facilities located in ul. Cypriana Kamila Norwida (2008) and Aqua Park in ul. Piłsudskiego, which is part of the indoor swimming pool managed by the Tarnów Sports and Recreation Centre (2010), were opened to the public. New large retail and service buildings have emerged on the city’s landscape. The first was Galeria Tarnovia, which opened in November 2009 in ul. Krakowska. It covered an area of 36.5 thousand square metres. Shortly afterwards, in 2010, the 80,000 square metre Gemini Jasna Park shopping centre was opened in the Jasna housing estate.503 In November 1999, the Tarnowskie Towarzystwo Budownictwa Społecznego (Tarnów Social Housing Association) was established to support housing construction. The Association delivered its first block of flats two years later.504

The determination of the city authorities to stop the deurbanisation of Tarnów is evidenced by the fact that the City Development Strategy – Tarnów 2020 was announced and adopted by the City Council on 30 June 2011 (Resolution No. XI/111/2011).505 One of the objectives set forth was the adoption of packages aimed at enhancing the entrepreneurial spirit among Tarnów residents. In the urban context, several key ideas were adopted, including raising the standard of urban infrastructure, expanding the so-called leisure infrastructure, improving the aesthetics of urban spaces and, finally, increasing the attractiveness of the housing offer. The latter goal was to be achieved by supporting the construction of social rental housing. The plan aimed to build upon the principles guiding the activities of the Tarnowskie Towarzystwo Budownictwa Społecznego (Tarnow Social Housing Association) mentioned above.506 The depopulation of Tarnów observed since the beginning of the century undoubtedly remains one of the greatest threats to the city’s development, also in spatial terms. The current and future city authorities face numerous challenges and ambitious tasks aimed at reversing these unfavourable processes. To this end, on 15 September 2022, the City Council of Tarnów adopted a resolution approving the document entitled City Development Strategy – Tarnów 2030.507 In addition to economic and social is- 502 Miasto Tarnów, [in:] Statystyczne vademecum samorządowca, Kraków 503 K. Moskal, Kronika Tarnowa (as n. 452), pp. 291, 294, 296–297. 504 Ibidem, p. 268. 505 Strategia rozwoju miasta Tarnów 2020: aktywny, komfortowy, silny, 506 Ibidem, pp. 7, 13, 16. 507 Resolution No. LXX/679/2022 of the Tarnow City Council of 15 September 2022 on the adoption of the City Development Strategy – Tarnów 2030. sues, the document focuses on the spatial and physical development of the city. The main assumptions in this regard include the need to modernise the city’s infrastructure and to develop systemic measures aimed at stopping negative trends such as depopulation of central housing estates, lack of competitiveness in the housing market due to the old building stock, as well as ‘the decreasing ‘city­forming’ role of the city centre and its impact on the city and its surroundings.’508 In the light of the presented strategy, seven types of spatial layouts have been distinguished within the city boundaries, including old town development, inner-city development constructed in the 18th and 19th centuries, high-rise multi-family development, low-rise multi-family development, contemporary (orderly) single-family development, single-family development based on the layout of former villages which renders them disorderly, and finally industrial and commercial development.509

Given the factor of sustainable development, green areas remain an important part of the urban space. Currently, the ‘managed green areas’ comprise historical parks (Strzelecki, Sanguszków, Kwiatkowskiego, and Planty Kolejowe) and parks that do not currently have the status of a monument. These include Park Sośnina, Park Legionów, Park na Górze św. Marcina (St. Martin’s Hill Park), and Park Zbylitowska Góra. These green areas are complemented by ‘areas of natural character’, such as the area around Stawy Krzyskie (Krzyskie Ponds), Las Lipie (Lipie Forest), and the Debrza Reserve. Recreational areas also include fifteen allotment gardens within the city limits and fourteen cemeteries, six of which are World War I necropolises.510 1. The Old Town of Tarnów, with its highly valuable historical urban layout and architecture, playing a key role in the central area of Tarnów. 2. The downtown area, including Plac Kościuszki and the railway station, with developed frontages and services, serving as the central area of the city. 3. St. Martin’s Hill, along with the open areas at its foothills – the region around ul. Lotnicza, which constitutes an important natural, cultural, and recreational space in Tarnów. 4. The area of the Nitrogen Works in Mościce and its surroundings, regarded as one of the most significant elements in the employment structure of the inhabitants, the spatial structure of the city, as well as its history. 5. Emerging local centres in various parts of the city, requiring clear delineation and, as far as possible, provision of a comprehensive range of basic services. 6. Green areas, including wooded and recreational areas, characterised by a patchwork layout, requiring supplementation, interconnection, and the addition of various forms of intensive urban greenery, mainly parks and wooded parks of recreational significance. 7.National and international transportation routes, represented by the A4 motorway and its junctions, as well as national roads 94 and 73.511 508 Strategia Rozwoju Miasta – Tarnów 2030 (City Development Strate- The action strategy covering the years 2022–2030 envisages the proper protection of the designated areas by raising their standards and ensuring their synergistic interconnection. Taking into account specific measures, the plans include, among other things, the development of residential construction, strengthening the city’s environmental system, and simultaneously structuring economic activity zones such as the Tarnów Industrial Cluster. Ultimately, the eastern and northern regions of Tarnów, including the estates of Rzędziny, Gumniska, Stru-

sina, Krzyż, and Klikowa, are planned for (residential) urbanisation. While considering Tarnów’s development prospects in the coming years, the city authorities have not ruled out expanding the city limits to areas adjacent to the administrative boundaries but have not specified the exact directions of such incremental urbanisation.512 The development of Tarnów has changed over time, partly due to destructive fires and wartime activities. Despite this, many buildings have survived to the present day, either protected by legal forms of monument preservation or listed in the local register of monuments. The city, rich in historical sites, has been the subject of numerous studies, ranging from inventories and catalogues to scientific, dictionary-style, and popular publications. This section serves as a synthesis and supplement to the preceding map, with the aim of highlighting the multistage nature of the city’s urban development. What follows is a discussion of the objects that currently stand out as distinctive landmarks in the urban cityscape.513 513 In the compilation, I used, among others, records from the Regional Office for the Protection of Monuments, the team of Immovable Monuments Documentation at the National Heritage Institute (green and white cards), architectural-conservation studies, and architectural expertise. Built between 1329 and 1342, the castle was thoroughly rebuilt and extended by Jan Amor Tarnowski in the 16th century and then divided into (1) a Gothic castle with two round towers and (1) a Renaissance bastioned fortification. The Gothic castle consisted of a cylindrical stone tower, a residential part with a chapel and outbuildings. In the 16th century, the residential part was remodelled into a Renaissance palace. The fortress was modernised, including the construction of a two-storey arsenal with barrel-vaulted chambers inside the walls and the fortification of the walls with roundels. In 1570, the castle was reduced to ruins by an invasion. In 1603, Janusz Ostrogski added a short wing to the Upper Castle. In the 17th century, the fortress was divided into the Upper Castle, a courtyard, and other buildings. At that time, it served not only as the residence of the town’s lords but also as the seat of the Starosty. In 1675, further renovations were carried out, but the castle was already in ruins. In 1747, Janusz Aleksander Sanguszko authorised the demolition of the castle walls and allocated the materials for the construction of a church in the Bernardine monastery in Tarnów. Further parts of the castle walls disappeared in 1848, the stones and bricks being used for private projects of the Sanguszko family. ­Zubrzycki. The brick building, which dates back to the mid-14th century, underwent significant renovations in the 16th century (mentioned in 1526 and then in 1558–1561), in the 19th century (including 1850, 1861–1862, 1865, 1879, 1889–1892), in 1925–1929 (reconstruction of certain elements of architectural details), in 1947, and 1964–1968. During the latter period, the building underwent extensive restoration work ‘with the aim of restoring it to its 16th-century state’ for museum exhibition purposes (rebuilding of the façade, changes to the arrangement of the window openings, relocation of the main portal, replacement of the pinnacles and installation of a ribbed ceiling over the Commoner Room). Between 1558 and 1561, the Town Hall took on a Mannerist appearance. The Town Hall’s cellar housed, among other things, an armoury. On the ground floor, there were vaulted rooms (including wietnica (an assembly hall), the residence of the municipal instigator and a dwelling of a wietnik (a person in charge of the assembly hall)). On the upper floor, there was, among other things, the Commoner Room (rebuilt into smaller rooms in 1793) and the Council Room. The building suffered serious fires in 1663 and 1792. After the second fire, it was rebuilt, but the ceilings were lowered, and the layout of the rooms changed. In 1861–1862, the cellars of the Town Hall (unused since the 18th century) were uncovered, the western corner of the town scale was demolished (it was completely dismantled during subsequent renovations), and the entire building underwent urgent repairs. In 1889–1892, Szczęsny Zaremba supervised a thorough renovation and redesign of the building in the Neo-Renaissance style. The current development around the main square (Rynek) is considerably less rich than before the fire of 1663. Still, many of the townhouses standing at the market today have cellars dating from the 14th, 15th, and 16th centuries, e.g. the cellars in the Ratajewicz’s townhouse date from the 14th century. The slow reconstruction of the crisis-ridden town, the merging of plots of land and a series of fires caused the buildings to change their appearance. Modest tenement houses replaced the magnificent Renaissance townhouses with arcades. The arcades remaining after fires and reconstructions were later completely removed or rebuilt. The arcades in the Rosowski and Sakowiczowska townhouses at Rynek 14 and between the townhouses at Rynek 19–21 were recreated as a result of restoration and conservation works in the 20th century. At the end of the 18th century and in the first decades of the 19th century, after fires, many townhouses were extended with a second floor. At that time, they were also given a new style, such as Nikielson’s townhouse, which was transformed into a broad-fronted building with Neoclassical decoration. At the turn of the 19th and 20th centuries, the townhouses were further remodelled, and many were given historicist facades.

The building was constructed from the 14th century onwards on the site of its predecessor, originally a single-nave parish church with a closed rectangular chancel. It was enlarged after 1400, probably with the addition of a tower, two chapels (sacristy and St. Cross) and a chapel of St. Anne in the early 15th century. A two-storey Gothic chapel (rebuilt in 1712, covered with a dome and decorated in the Baroque style) and the Chapel of the Commission of the Apostles were added in 1415. Between 1485 and 1514, the church underwent further extensions financed by Jan Amor Tarnowski, with late Gothic portals, additional stone elements of architectural ornamentation, vaults (including the net vault of the nave from the 16th century, added in 1890) and a new chapel – Our Lady of the Scapular (around 1514, with a cross-rib vault), together with the treasury above the sacristy. The collegiate church suffered fires in 1617, 1663, and 1735, but the generosity of the nobility and townspeople made it possible to repair and renovate the damaged parts. Between 1810– 1816 and 1827–1832, the church was transformed from a single nave with chapels to a triple nave with arcades between the naves. The chancel was extended and a neo-Gothic chapel of St. Benedict was added. In the 1850s, new altars were purchased, the floor was laid, and the so-called canonical sacristy was built. On the initiative of Bishop Ignacy Łobos, architect Julian Zachariewicz prepared a plan for the purist restoration of the Cathedral in 1889–1897. During this period, the last bay of the chancel with a polygonal closure, two northern porches and the crown of the tower were added. The neo-Gothic stylistic layer was applied in a purist spirit. The church was renovated several times: in 1926–1927, in 1957–1960 (conservation of the tombs, replacement of the lighting and flooring, exposition of the Gothic windows in the chancel, frescoes around the Ostrogski monuments and Gothic-Renaissance polychromy in the chapel of Our Lady of the Scapular), in 1960–1962 ( renovation of the polychromy and flooring), in 1983 (conservation and protection of the polychromy) and 2005–2007 (replacement of the roof).

The space of the square, which was already marked out at the time of the city’s foundation in 1330, is currently dominated by the cathedral. The most important buildings on the square (apart from the Cathedral) include the Scholasteria, the Akademiola, the Mikołajowski House, Canonry I and Canonry II, and the Canon’s Palace, surrounded by buildings from the 19th and 20th centuries. The Mikołajowski House was owned by the Koruszowski family and Barbara and Jan Mikołajowski using the Gryf coat of arms. In 1524, the latter carried out an extensive late Gothic reconstruction. After Wojciech Kaszewicz founded the so-called Akademiola in 1753, the house became the residence of the professors of the academic colony. In 1792, when a gymnasium replaced the academy, the building became the residence of the prefect of the gymnasium. In the following decades, the Mikołajowski House was used for educational purposes and temporarily housed a health centre. After renova- tions in 1946–1952, it was converted into an exhibition hall for the Diocesan Museum. Next to it is the Mansjonarzy House, which assumed its present form in the 18th century. In the 1960s and 1990s, it underwent construction and adaptation works (for museum purposes among others), including the construction of a staircase, the replacement of windows and doors, and the adaptation of the ceiling structure for exhibition purposes. The canon’s brick palace, a two-storey building erected along the defensive walls by Father Mikołaj Zamoyski, was extensively rebuilt by Prepositus Stanisław Świejkowski. After the partitions of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, it housed the circular authorities. In the last two decades of the 18th century, two side wings were added, and a coach house was organised in one of the wings. In the 19th century, it underwent a thorough reconstruction, during which its external elevations were given NeoRenaissance forms. The filial Church of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary “on Burek” (currently the Sanctuary of Our Lady of the Scapular) The present temple was built on the outskirts of the city around 1458, replacing its predecessor. Consecrated in 1462, it has a single nave with a narrower, three-sided chancel closed to the north by a sacristy with a vestibule. There is a tower to the west. The church was badly damaged by fire in the early 17th century, but the burnt sections were rebuilt before 1640. Originally, three window openings decorated with stained glass from 1596 depicting saints (including St. Christopher and St. Paul) provided light to the interior. In 1620, two further windows were added to the chancel (on the south and north sides). The nave and chancel are covered by a common roof, and a spire tower was added in 1653. A new tower was built around 1910. The church was renovated in 1854 and then in 1963–1965 according to the design by architect Lech Stachowski. The interior houses a preserved 16th-century polychrome painting depicting the Tree of Jesse and paintings by Tadeusz Terlecki from 1930.

The church was built between 1595 and 1597, consecrated in 1597, but thoroughly rebuilt between 1857 and 1858. It is an oriented building with a nave wider and higher than the chancel closed by a three-sided apse. Inside, many elements of the original furnishings have been preserved, including a painting of the Holy Trinity from around 1600 and a Crucifixion with the cross-worshipping founders and the date of the building’s consecration given on a side altar from the late 16th century. The polychrome painting dates from the early 20th century. The church was renovated in 1965–1966 and 1996–1998. The complex of the Church of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross and the Bernardine monastery When the Bernardines arrived in Tarnów in 1459, a wooden church and monastery had already been prepared for them, later replaced by late Gothic brick buildings in 1468. The develop- ment was dominated by a single-nave church dedicated to Our Lady of the Snows with a narrower polygonally closed chancel and an adjoining three-winged monastery with a central courtyard. At present, only a few remains from this period are preserved, including fragments of the original chancel decoration and a portal of the former church tower. After in the 1780s the Bernardines moved into the buildings formerly occupied by the Bernardine nuns the existing complex of monastic church and convent suffered considerable damage, especially during fires in 1809 and 1814. Between 1823 and 1825, the eastern and western wings of the monastery were demolished. The only remnant of the original Bernardine structures is the building at ul. Bernardyńska 19, a fragment of the southern wing of the monastery rebuilt in the Neoclassical style in 1823. The convent at ul. Bernardyńska 13 was built in 1680 and originally belonged to the Bernardine Sisters, who had been living in Tarnów since 1555. The convent was originally attached to a wooden church from around 1630, which was replaced in 1752–1776 by a brick building dedicated to the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, founded by Paweł and Barbara Sanguszko. The single nave has a narrower chancel (both the nave and the chancel have two bays that are not exactly on the same axis of the church) due to the course of the street. The hall church, lit by windows on the south side, is covered by a saddle roof with varying heights. On the north wall of the chancel was the treasury (since 1954, the Chapel of Jesus the Merciful), on the south wall was the sacristy, and to the west of the nave was the convent oratory (now the music choir). Renovations were carried out in 1954, and the polychromy was restored in 1960 (by Karol Pustelnik). A reinforced concrete staircase to the choir was built in 1980, and marble floors were laid in 1987. The monastery grounds are bounded by a brick and plaster fence, with access through a gate (in the recess of the fence) on the western side.

A complex of buildings remodelled or built between 1877 and 1931, including the convent and school buildings (at ul. Bema 9 and 11), a dormitory (at ul. J. Bema 13; originally from the first half of the 19th century, extended in 1878 and 1898), and the remains of a 19th-century garden. These include a statue of the Immaculate Conception of the Virgin Mary from 1880, a statue of St. Joseph with the Child from 1891, and fragments of fences and farmyard buildings from the early 20th century. In 1877, seventeen nuns arrived in Tarnów. They settled in a onestorey house donated by Canon Karol Kraus and Maria Wittler (now ul. Bema 13). Karol Polityński built a church for the sisters in 1877–1878 and adapted the acquired property to the needs of the congregation. In 1884, at the initiative of the Ursuline Sisters, St. Ursula’s School was built according to Antoni Schmitzek’s plans ( ul. Bema 11). Between 1885 and 1889, a twostorey enclosure building designed by Schmitzek was erected. In 1889, the second floor of the building (now at ul. Bema 13), designed by Franciszek Hackbeil, was added. This was the beginning of the school’s extension (at the present ul. Bema 11) designed by Jan Lewiński from Lviv. In 1898, the first house donated to the Ursulines was extended by an additional floor. In 1903 and 1906, outbuildings and walls were erected, and in 1907, a two-storey wing was added to the school building. In the early 1920s, the convent complex consisted of the enclosure, the chapel, and the two-storey school building. In 1924, the wing of the school building (ul. Bema 11) was completed, and the whole complex included a chapel, four townhouses, and a garden. In 1931, a new school building designed by Edward Okoń was built. The representatives of the Missionaries of St. Vincent de Paul settled in Tarnów in 1904, and their temporary church was a wooden temple on Burek. The actual buildings of the Missionary Church-Monastery complex were designed by Jan Sas-Zubrzycki and constructed by builders under the direction of August Tarkowski on the land donated to the Congregation by Prince Eustachy Sanguszko. The Neo-Gothic church dedicated to the Holy Family was built between 1904 and 1908 as a brick structure on a base of sandstone quarried in Ciężkowice, with the upper parts of the walls made of brick. The church was consecrated on 4 October 1908 by Bishop Leon Wałęga. Around 1910, the area around the church was paved with ‘cement slabs,’ creating clear pathways. Renovations were carried out after the Second World War to repair war damage from 1944. The churchyard is marked by the original wall, although heavily modified in the 1960s, and a small shrine from the first half of the 19th century. An integral part of the complex is the current rectory, once a monastery with living quarters, a refectory, and a kitchen. It ceased to serve its original purpose after the construction of two new parish buildings in 1976 and 1985. The monastery building was consecrated and officially inaugurated on 23 May 1908.

The dedication refers to the original patrocinium and the image of Our Lady of Perpetual Succour, brought from Rome in 1914 and venerated in the church. Originally, a wooden cross stood on the site of the present church, followed by a small chapel built in 1883–1884 as a votive offering for the cessation of the plague that struck the inhabitants of Krzyż, a village near Tarnów, in 1873. The chapel was designed by Józef Szebest and consecrated on 21 September 1884 by Father Stanislaw Walczyński, canon of the Tarnów cathedral chapter. In 1909–1910, the chapel was extended by the master mason Jan Marek according to the design of Augustyn Tarkowski. The enlarged sacral building became a small church, where a separate parish of the Holy Cross was established on 10 May 1925. After 1945, the damaged walls were in danger of collapsing, and the incorporation of Krzyż into the municipality of Tarnów in 1958 resulted in the spatial and demographic development of the district. The new church was built between 1968 and 1971 on the foundations of the old one as a three-nave church with a tower at the front. It was consecrated in 1975. The square and the bimah are the remains of the Old Synagogue, which stood on the site until 1941. It was burnt down on 8 November 1939 and blown up and demolished two years later. At first, a wooden synagogue from 1582 stood in its place, serving the needs of the small Jewish population of Tarnów. It was probably destroyed by fire in the first decades of the 17th century and replaced by a brick building. The structure suffered successive fires, and permissions for new constructions were granted in 1661 and 1670. The last was extended in 1796 when the western vestibule and the northern extension were added (they burnt down in 1814). It was an example of a central synagogue. Further extensions took place between 1815 and 1848 (the synagogue was extended to the west, and the surrounding space was developed into a kind of synagogue complex). In the 1870s and 1880s, it received a Neo-Romanesque front. At the beginning of the 20th century, the area around the synagogue was fenced in. In 1929, a wooden vestibule was added. The remaining bimah was given a protective roof in 1987 and incorporated into a planned space to commemorate the synagogue.

Constructed in the final two decades of the 18th century on the site of the Sanguszkos’ wooden inn. Originally, the Baroque Ducal House of Hieronim Sanguszko had two wings and three storeys, and its surroundings included stables, among other features. Alongside the townhouse known as Książęca (Ducal), the palace was the second building in Tarnów connected with the Sanguszko residence. In 1825, the state authorities acquired the building, transforming it into the seat of the circular and later poviat authorities. The building was reconstructed in the 1830s and 1870s. At the turn of the 19th and 20th centuries, its layout and appearance were adapted to the needs of the circular and poviat authorities. During the latter reconstruction, the façade was given a Neo-Baroque form. Szczęsny Zaremba, as Tarnów’s director of construction, imbued the building with the character of a stylistically unified structure, aligning with the prevailing architectural trends of the monarchy. Of the defensive structures that have survived to the present day, the oldest date from the 14th to 16th centuries. Today, they include a two-storey late Gothic brick and stone half-roundel from the 16th century with preserved semicircular inward-flared embrasures, a brick tower with an original vault and traces of embrasures, and c. 400 metres of preserved town fortifications – walls and bailey (in 1959 there were only 15 sections), whose construction is dominated by zendrówka brick, laid in monk or/and Gothic bond. Based on this, it is known that the defensive walls of Tarnów formed an irregular oval, adapted to the topography of the area of the present Old Town. In the years 1648–1651, the fortifications were thoroughly renovated, with the last works being mentioned in the 1780s, when the fortifications were already obsolete and no longer fulfilled their primary function. In the last decade of the 18th century and the beginning of the 19th century, the Tarnów fortifications were demolished, and their remains were described as ruins in 1959. Their condition began to improve between 1961 and 1965 when they were secured and made accessible between 1954 and 1969. The park was established on the site of the former Podwale Dyksonówka town grange. Designed by Antoni Schmidt, a gardener from Krosno, it was constructed in 1866 and divided into a walking area and an agricultural part (with the western section further divided into a nursery and a vegetable garden). The Rifle Society’s shooting range and its surroundings (located in the southwestern part of the park, designed by Janusz Rypuszyński in 1891) are integral components of the park. The Neo-Gothic shooting range (circa 1866), the orangery (circa 1894, reconstructed in 1929, 1936, and 1955), the greenhouse (1878), the two-room house, and the wooden gatekeeper’s booth (circa 1873, later replaced by a gatekeeper’s lodge), a gardener’s house in the Vienna Secession style (1902–1907, designed by Szczęsny Zaremba, replacing an earlier one from 1894), a water fountain (1912), a mausoleum (1928), and a water chime by the Viennese firm J. A. Hilpert all constitute significant features. In 1912, the location of the main entrance was changed, altering the spatial layout, including the introduction of a strip-and-group tree planting system. In 1927–1928, the park’s layout and appearance were modified to suit the function of the mausoleum of General Józef Bem (designed by Adolf Szyszko-Bohusz). In 1927, the entire area was enclosed by a concrete fence with a representative entrance gate (secessionist fittings designed by E. Okoń). After the Second World War, the streets were asphalted, electric lighting was installed in 1955, and the orangery buildings were renovated and adapted for social housing.

Originally, the building was to be called the Hotel Polski, but it eventually became the Hotel Bristol, owned by the Rypuszyński family. The establishment was built between 1904 and 1906 according to the design of Janusz Rypuszyński. It represents the characteristic features of the architect’s early style, influenced by Art Nouveau and geometric forms. Due to the configuration of the site, the building has a distinctive layout and plan. In the 1930s, the building was extended and the façade facing ul. Krakowska was redesigned by Witold Giżbert-Studnicki. Art Nouveau decorations were replaced by eclectic style. Further alterations took place in 1941–1942 when the building was adapted for use as a hotel for Germans, according to a design by the office of A. Seifert and M. Elckmayer. Subsequently, from 1949 to 1962, the building underwent a series of adaptations and modernisations. The building was designed by Karol Polityński and built in 1880–1882 as the headquarters of the Tarnów Savings Bank (on the first floor) and the Casino and Music Societies (on the second floor). In 1896, the building was extended according to the project of Adolf Stapf when, among other things, one of the wings was extended, and the layout of the building was changed. In 1929, the wooden structure of the main staircase was replaced by an iron-concrete one, adapting it to the needs of the building, which had both banking and cultural functions. In 1949, the building was renovated to accommodate the Polish United Workers’ Party (PZPR), new partitions were installed, and terracotta floors were replaced with parquet. The interior walls were also painted. Renovation of the Hall of Mirrors took place in 1964, while conservation of the interior decoration – stucco, stonework, and window woodwork – was carried out in 2011–2013. The one-storey, two-bay wooden mansion with a full cellar and the so-called ‘Polish’ high hipped roof was mentioned as early as the end of the 18th century. Over time, the wooden walls were replaced by brick walls. It stands as a testament to the former development of Krakowskie Przedmieście, which included the Sanguszko Inn from 1799 (on the site of the former Rhod Inn behind the Krakowska Gate; after reconstruction, it became the Hotel Krakowski) or the Post Office building with a stagecoach station. Since 1903, the property has been owned by the city, and in 1927, it became the site of the municipal museum. It was thoroughly renovated in the 1970s. It is surrounded by a garden with a wooden granary from the late 18th century.

The Neoclassical mansion was built at the beginning of the 19th century as a two-bay, one-storey wooden structure. There is a four-columned portico on the facade. Over time, a brick extension with a suite room arrangement was added to the northern elevation. In the 1930s, the wooden walls were replaced by brick walls. In 1959, the building was classified as severely damaged, but repairs were undertaken, and in 1966 it was classified as partially damaged. The property was sold to the State Treasury in 1975. A new fence was built at the end of the 1970s. It is a Neoclassical building from the first half of the 19th century with the characteristics of a suburban residence. The Kostaś family lived here, including Eustachy Sanguszko’s majordomo, Tadeusz Kostaś, who received the property from Prince Eustachy. In 2018–2020, the mansion, which was in ruins, underwent a general renovation and the building was turned into a restaurant space. Stadtplan Tarnow. Scale 1: 5,000, colour print, dimensions 96 × 77 cm. Depicts the state in August 1944, during the German occupation of the city. Prepared for internal use, according to a declaration based on a cadastral plan from the 19th century. Major German street names, squares, important public buildings and churches are marked, as well as roads, railway lines, hydrographic network, and green areas. No legend. Original: National Archives in Kraków, ref. no. 29/663/0/6/971. Scale 1:10,000, colour manuscript on ozalide copy, dimensions 106 × 84 cm. Fragment of a genealogical table of the Tarnowski family, woodcut, 55.51 × 75.99 cm. Augustinus Thille Sculpus, Łavrea siuc [sic] arbor. Tarnoviana, reprinted by A. Piliński, Paryż 1872. View of Tarnów from the south. Behind the double line of ramparts, through which a gate in the tower leads (the tower and the gate at the exit of ul. Wielkie Schody), the town hall building with a tower, the collegiate church and the Bernardine monastery are immortalised among the conventionally depicted buildings. The hospital and the Church of the Holy Ghost can be seen in front of the walls, next to the road leading to the gate. Original: National Archives in Kraków, Tarnów Branch, and other records; see: St. Potępa, Tarnów w dawnych rysunkach i obrazach, Tarnów 2007, pp. 19–21. Zygmunt Vogel, watercolour, dimensions 42.8 × 58.5 cm. View of the market square from the south. In addition to the Town Hall and the townhouses next to the market square, the non-existent buildings of plac Katedralny are immortalised in the background. Original: Regional Museum in Tarnów.

2.3. Tarnów. The Collegiate Church, 1800 Zygmunt Vogel, watercolour 43 × 58 cm. View from the south-west towards the church, the collegiate buildings and the northern part of today’s plac Kazimierza Wielkiego. Original: Regional Museum in Tarnów. Teofil Czyszkowski, watercolour, dimensions 7.5 × 15.1. View of Tarnów from the south, showing the town with the town hall, the cathedral and the as yet not rebuilt Bernardine church, the buildings of Przedmieście Krakowskie with the Hotel Krakowski. The space in between is filled with urban, storied development that does not adhere to scale. The visible buildings include the Krakowski Hotel, the cathedral, and the Bernardine monastery and convent complexes. Original: Museum in Nowy Sącz, inven. no. MNS/1465/S; A. Ky dryńska, Zabytki Ziemi Krakowskiej w Sztambuchu Czyszkowskich „Materiały i Sprawozdania Województwa Krakowskiego” (1970). Sepia drawing, approx. 23 × 17.6 cm. View of Tarnów from the south, showing considerable expansion of suburban development (compared to Czyszkowski’s view) in the area of ul. Bernardyńska. The Bernardine Church, closing the panorama from the east, has already received its Neoclassical appearance. National Archives in Kraków, Zbiory kartograficzne, ref. no. VI 436 (former Tarnów RM 5); see: St. Potępa, Tarnów w dawnych rysunkach i obrazach, pp. 28, 34. Topographic map of Poland in the 1992 system, GUGiK, National Geoportal – WMTS service.
